A GENERAL, an old bachelcr, had a habit of .cleaning his knife and fork at the table before using. At a dinner he indulged in this habit. The hostess at. once sent him another set. The general ,repeated the scene, and the waiter brought a third set. The general became furious. "Shall I clean the knives and forks for the entire company?" he cried.

Oriz day, as a doctor was on his rounds, he hap- pened to meet one of his patients, an old man over 90 years of age, who was an inveterate smoker. "Dear me!" said the doctor, "you are smoking again, and yet you know it is slow poison ?I'" The old man took his pipe out of his mouth solemnly, shook his head, and replied: "Yes, sir, I think it must be, for I've been at it for 70 years, and I'm not dead yet!"

A BUMPICI'N'S IDEA OF ART.—When the late Sir IJohn Millais was taking sketches on the Tay, near Kinfauns Station, for his famous picture, "Chill October," a countryman watched him for a while, ,and then ventured to ask, "Did ye never try pho- Itographin' ? " "No," replied the late President of Ithe Royal Academy, "I never took a photograph." '" Man ! it's a peety," replied the bumpkin, eyeing the-unfinished sketch, "for it's a vast quicker; and lit's mare liker, tae !" This is a true story, I believe, and Sir John is said to have told it with great glee. ABSENT' MINDED. —Probably the worst instance of absence of mind is that reconled of a well-known University professor. He had gone to spend the evening-at a friend's house. When he was about to leave it was raining very heavily, and the hostess kindly offered him accommodation for the night, which he readily accepted. Suddenly the guest disappeared, nobody knowing what had become of him. The family were about to retire for the night when Professor X— walked in, as wet-as a drowned. rat. He had been home to fetch his night attire!

"D"-ocron, one moment, please 1" exclaimed a man, who came running in just as a physician was disappearing into his consulting-room. "I'll see you shortly, sir." "But a second is all I want." • You must, wait your turn," repeated the doctor sternly, as he, shut the door behind him. The -visitor took a seat in the reception-room, read the 'papers, looked at the pictures, played with the dog, and nearly 30 minutes had passed before the. doctor reappeared and with an air of condescension said: "I am at your service. Your turn has come. "What can Ido for you?" "Oh, nothing in particular," was tip- reply. "I just dropped in to tell you that three strange cows are in your garden and are having a picnic." As IT OCTIIIT.—A lady once purchased, of a well- known firm in London, a very handsome Brussels carpet. After having it down in her drawing- room for a few weeks, numbers of the little threads of which it was composed began, to her surprise, to work up, and gave it the appearance of having been scratched all over by a cat. She accordingly wrote at once and complained, but was greatly amused on receiving the following reply : " MADAM,—We are very sorry that you have not found the carpet satisfactory; but are you not :aware that it is the sign of a really good Brussels to sprout ?—We remain, Madam, Yrs., etc."

SIMPLE. —lf the following story is to be believed, the Boers reputation for shrewdness in business matters must considerably suffer. A Boer farmer asked seventy thousand pounds for a piece of land, but this amount the would-be purchaser affected to consider too small. "To-morrow," said he, "I will pay you one hundred thousand pounds in hard cash." The Boer assented, and on the follow- ing day, when the deed of sale had been duly signed and witnessed, the purchaser produced two bags of sovereigns, and counted out the contents of the smaller of the two. "Here," said he, is one hun- dred pounds." "Yes, said the Boer. "And here," pursued the other, counting out the contents of the second bag, "is one thousand pounds." "Yes, said the Boer. " Well, that's a hundred thousand.' "Yes," said the Boer, and the bargain was com- pleted to the satisfaction of the latter.

A ora•rrurmaN, returning from abroad, brought a very expensive lace shawl for his wife and was desirous of avoiding the necessity of adding to its coat by paying duty. On board the steamer was an exceedingly attractive lady to whom, when they neared land he confided his dilemma. "Why my good sir," she said naïvely, "that is no, dilemma at all. I will wear the shawl ashore, and then no questions will be asked." The gentleman paid a glowing tribute to the wonderful fertility of the feminine mind, and accepted the offer. The shawl graced the lady's shoulders, and was cer- tainly very becoming. The trunks were examined and passed, and then the gentleman saluted the lady,spoke of the pleasure he had enjoyed in hernmpany, hoped they would have the pleasure ,of crossing the sea again, and, then asked for the shawl she had smuggled through so smartly. "I se`but l ywohea th ave oshawlon, dtoo beg your par(, she saitdh,e h von refer to. " "Why, Le sure," he naturally answered. "And why stliould I give you my shawl ?" she inquired. The 'dialogue waxed so warm that she had to threaten to send for a policeman unless he desisted; and since he could not legally claim the shawl without convicting himself of a deliberate attempt to swindle the Government, he was compelled to leave With the stranger the present which he had intended for his wife.

Fruits and poppies are the chief things used on the most fashionable hats. In the milliners' win- dows are hats bedecked with poppies, and toques or straws are ornamented with fruit, foliage, and either ribbon or some soft material, such as 3hlffoo or gauze. Those who possess sunburnt straws, Panamas and Leghorns, should at once adopt the fashionable trimming of scarlet poppies, relieved with black satin or chiffon, and further elaborated by graceful wheatears.

A smart toque is of crumpled fancy straw, pierced at the sides with two long gilt millinery pins, crossed towards the centre and headed with pear-shaped pearls. There is a large rose in front, and tinted ostrich tips at the side. Toques of the beefeater type, draped with chiffon, and covered with embroidered or sequined tulle, are still popular, and look like being revived with autumn gowns. They are in- variably trimmed at the left side with clusters of feathers or high bows and osprey, and flowers, or choux of velvet or chiffon nestle under the brim. Later on, velvet hats will be made in similar fashion, but just now the poppy headgear or the sailor hat with wings demand attention. There are always two kinds of sailor hat, the strictly nautical, with big brim and simple band, or the smart sailor, with an amplitude of wings, quills and ribbon.

Dainty cordings of white, red, or amber are the favoured trimmings for serges, and blouses of shot blue and rose, blue and amber, and other combi- nations are preferred in glace silks, trimmed with narrow ruches or minute frills of white or yellow ribbon. A shot blue and yellow glac4 blouse had a pouched vest of yellow silk, covered with soft net of antique tint, and a plenitude of tucks divided into groups by tiny frills of yellow ribbon. Many very stylish blouses are made in grenadine or washable materials such as lawn, and trimmed with lace.

Foulard skirts are being worn with white muslin blouses, lavishly inserted with lace, and worn over slips of glace or plain foulard matching the skirt in colour. The new skirts, to look stylish. need pronounced hips, and the manufacturer, always on the qui vive, has already provided hip. bustles, which supply the necessary contour. At present the hip-bustle is too exaggerated for all but the very slightest figures, but the up-to-date modiste is introducing small rouleaux of horse-hair on the hips, under the sheath-like skirt, and a straight fan at the back, folded like a single box. pleat aboub four to six inches broad.

A fashionable costume is made of "Grand Duchess," a beautiful poplin, with a very hand- some wavy design in silk. A pale leaf-green, a heliotrope, an electric-blue, and a lovely shade of fawn can be had in this material, which has all the appearance of a very rich brocaded silk, but would wear very much longer, and drape more gracefully. The trimmings are of beige guipure lace, and the waistcoat is of crinkle creamy chiffon, with a cravat of beige lace edging at the throat. This model would also look well in the "Queen's Royal," and it could be carried out in cashmere or thin faced cloth with good effect, or in a light fancy material for a less expensive gown, such as the "Rosalie" or the " Ruddigore." A very effective plaid blouse is charming in red and white cotton, with collar of red twill or silk, and over this, when required, a collar of white linen or lace-trimmed cambric can be worn. The opening is filled in with a little habit shirt, with either a stand-up or turn-down collar. This blouse only requires three and a half yards of plaid cotton and half a yard of twill, and can be !Bade entirely without lining. Blue and white plaid, with a blue sailor collar, outlined white braid, is charming with a serge skirt, and will suit those who prefer a quieter colour than scarlet, although this latter is very fashionable. The Eton coat is a fashion which is always modernised and brought up-to-date, and with the present tightly-fitted sleeves and skirts is peculiarly youthful and smart. A smart costume is of grey cashmere with the skirt lined yellow glad, left separate at the edge, and finished with a pleated frill of the same silk. The grey cashmere is simply hemmed up deeply and has a folded braid at the edge, and the trimming suggests a tablier skirt. This trimming is of white and grey braid, the grey forming large scrolls, and the white and more compact line of wheels. These braided trimmings can be bought by the yard, also silk passementerie is exceedingly effective, if selected in a straggling scroll design and partially laid over a floral insertion lace. Revers of the cashmere, mounted on canvass, turn back in front, and are outlined with the trimming, and the Eton coat is lined with yellow glace silk. Yours lovingly JENNIE.

The museum which has been established in the ancient Gatehouse of Cariebrooke Castle,as a memorial to Prince Henry of Battenberg, includes many objects pertaining to the perscesal life of the late Priace,and also some con- nected with his brief and fatal sojourn on the West Coast of Africa. This museum has taken two years to arrange, but it is now available for toe inspection of the ordinary Castle visitors,within certain hours. Princess Henry of Battenbere, Governor of the Isle of Wight,peir- formed the epeniug ceremony, adding thereby yet another sad function to the many it has been her lot to take part in of lase. The historic old Castle was parti- ally restored some years since.and is an interesting spot, much patronised by visitore,especially those of the acne - tour photographic persuasion. Mr:lcon:las Cochrane, Deputy-Governor of the Island, and custodian of Carisbrsoke Castle, is the younger San of the late Admiral Sir Thomas Cochrane,and is married to a sister of Lord Stradbroke. The family is retnarkab'e for the extraordinary variation in the ages of its mem- bers. Mrs. Ware Scott, who died last year, was eighty• three years old,and was half-sister to Ms. Cochrane woo is but forty-two. Although no gloat landowners, the Ccchranes fill one of the biggest social positions in the Priucess Henry will,it is said,visit the Czar and Czarina during the coming winter at SePetersbarg. The Priem: si is very much attached to her niece, a feeling which the yeung Empiess fully rsdprocates. Princess Henry's acquaintance with the Russian language is somewhat limited,but this is net likely to calve Her Royal Highness any icconvonience. English is very much spoken at the Russian Court,and the Princess speaks French and Ger- man fluently. It is a fact that no court in the world presents such a picturesque and magnificent appearance as does that of RUESia. The Russian Court military and ministerial dress is costly,and rich in the extreme. and this richness is carried out evente the liveries at the servants, their scarlet coats being literally ablaze with gold. At any function therefore,the show is brilliant, but more especi- ally perhaps at a ba.l, when the rich evenin4 toilettes of the women, enchanced by jewels of priceless worth, add much to the already brilliant effect. The Duke of Teck is causing his relatives and friends great anxiety. It was hoped his trip to Germany would have proved beneficial, but instead of this he has re- turned worse than before. There does not seam to ba any specific malady,only he lute drooped,and has seemed to have no interest in life since the death of the Duchess. A deetor and nurse are iii constant attendance now upon the Duke, and he is rarely seen out of doors,except in his invalid cnair. The Duchess of York, and Prince Adolphus of Teck, are unremitting in their attention to their fr Vier, but despite every ease and consideration, the Duke seems to grow weaker,and possess less hold on life, as time goes on. The Prince of Wales has made definite arrangements to build a house near Cromer, chiefly for the use of Princess Victoria, who fidds the Norfolk coast (specially beneficial to her health. The district is one of many places on the East Coast where the sea is breaking in on the land. The Cromer of ancient times is two or three miles out at sea,and when Doomsday Book was compiled its present position was the site of an inland town. At Sheringbam, a vessel drawing twenty feet of water can now ride at anchor where forty years since there was a cliff fifty feet high. Suffolk is also suffering in the seine manner, and sent presents many examples of serious encroachments of the sea. The same nrooess is a'so going along the coasts of Lincolnshire, Yorkshire, Northumberland, and on the East coast of Scotland. The first lighthouse at the mouth of the Tay was built on land which is now quite sneer - water. On the other hand there are many places where the sea is receding, and in some of these the sickle and the scythe are at work, where not long ago was the silt sea. The Dee Estuary in Cheshire has been lergely turnsd to account in this way, and a good dell of flat low-lying land has been reclaimed from the sea in Lincolnshire, Cambridgeshire and Norfolk. Apropos of lighthouses, their erection in this country bag not proceeded upon any systematic plan, but in nearly every case they have been constructed simply because of the disastrous losses that have occurred for want of them. Among the mere celebrated lighthouses of me darn times are the Eddyetene, the Bell Rook, the Skerrynore. the Bishop Rock, the Wolf Rock, Land's End, the Dhu Reartach Rock, and the Chicken Rock. The "Bishop," which rears its head from the Bishop Rock, six miles west of St. Agnes, the most westerly of the Scilly Isles, may be said to be one of the moat lonely. Thus lighthouse meets the lull force of ths Atlantic, and some idea of the strength required in such a build- ing.may be ob•ained from the fact that the massive bell which was fixed with strong iron supports built jute the masonrseat a height of one hundred and twenty feet above the level of the sea was struele in 1880, with such force by a wave that ran up the tower, that it was wrenched from its place and its supports broken. The most celebrated lighthouse of ancient times web that erected about 283 8.C.. on the island et Pharos, opposite to Alexandria, which endured for 1800 years. The celebrated Colossus of Rhodes has also been hasps posed by come to have had a lieht at its summit, or in its hand, but of this there is no certain evidence. There are ruins of many towers on the coasts of Great Britain, and en the shores of Europe, which are believed to las the remains of ancient lightdouses. For one thing it has the advantage of leaving the hostr!ss free to amuse ter guests, in the cer- tainty that nothing will go wrong, and another advan- tage it possesses is, that it supplies one of. the.etew formsin which a bachelor can return the hespitali...y of his married friends. A WARD OF THE KING.
BY KATHARINE S. MACQTJOID, Author of "Maisie Derrick," "The Story of Lois," "Patty," "Louisa," "At the Red Glove," "Miss Ryon of Eyoncourt," &c,
CHAPTER XV . ROLTAND'a QUIET.

Rolland de la Touche gave command of the troop to Mathieu, while with his own hands he entrusted to Lao the precious banner of the Kergrists. By the time he had ridden a league . with these two, in advance of the rest, he had learnt how useful they could be to him in his quest. They had both served under the Constable, and they were devoted to him. Mathieu had been born in the Bour- bonnais, and acknowledged no other Sovereicn ' than the Duke of Bourbon. They both detested the new Count of Laval, and Rolland found him- self compelled to hear many tales to the disadvan- tage of Jeanne's present guardian. Rolland's anxiety to rejoin the young Countess ,had greatly increased since he left Orbec ; he now .determined to give up his visit to Mayenne, because it would cause a considerable detour. He would travel to Moulins' 'by way of Vendome and Blois, because, having gathered that Jeanne had followed that route, he hoped, in one or other place, to glean some tidings as to where he should at last And her. He had no fear of ultimate failure; Rolland de In Touche had not an exalted- idea of his. own powers, but he firmly believed that there •was no such word as "impossible" in any enter- prise he undertook. He did not, however, give up his purpose of seeking for Gillonne ; he despatched Lao with one of his own men from Coetfrec to make inquiry for the woman at Mayenne, and if they found reason to suspect that she had gone on to Orbec, to follow her there, and to bring her on with all speed to • Moulins, where he would leave instructions at an inn recommended by Mathieu as to his subsequent route.

They travelled more quickly than Jeanne and her escort, for they changed horses more frequently, and spent most of their time in the saddle. At Moulins Rolland announced his intention of spending a few hours at the inn, called Le Com. Loyal, recommended by Mathieu, who said it was kept by his cousin, once a servant of the Duke of Bourbon. There would be clean beds, he said, and fair dealing.. "Good qualities both; if the food and wine are on the same level, we cannot do better," Rolland answered, so they rode down the steep street of the town to the inn where Jeanne and Laval had rested. Neither at Vendome nor Blois did they gain any tidings of the party from Laval. At Blois the Constable was in every man's mouth; he was stigmatised as a traitor who had sold his sword to Henry of England and to the Emperor Charles; so near Amboise the Royal influence was 13aramount. More than once the travellers heard the hope expressed that Bourbon would soon be taken, and then drawn and quartered, as a traitor to King and country. Rolland was forced to bind Mathieu down to keep the peace, so indignant was the honest fellow at the insults heaped on his bene- factor. The Vicomte rode along pensively_; he knew that if by any chance he encountered the Duke, who was said to be in hiding in the Bour- bonnais, his plain duty as a loyal subject was to deliver him up to justice; and he also new that he would rather cut off his own right hand than betray Charles of Bourbon to the Ring. He dismounted before the door of the Coeur Loyal, and noted the cordial greeting between Mathieu and the hostess. While he waited for supper, he bade the man inquire about the Countess and the party with whom she travelled. Mathieu did not return with his tidings, and Rolland sup- posed that they had put up at the wrong hostelry, and that he should have to make inquiry in Moulins itself. _ _

He had gone up to his bedchamber, and was sitting at the window looking up the rising road, when Mathieu knocked at the door; the man looked excited, but he did not speak till the Viconhe gave him leave. "My lord," he said eagerly, "the lady has been here; also the new Count of Laval." He went back to the door and looked out; then he opened the door into the loft. "At a time like this, my lord knows, lives hang on words. It appears that the lady herself told my cousin she was on her way to Lyons to see the King; my cousin, however, feels sure that the Count of Laval is engaged in tracking him you wot of, my lord, and that there- fore, instead of turning off to Lyons, the party has gone on towards Le Puy. But mark this, my lord; when the lady in the early morning left the hostel—'twas but three days ago—the Count of Laval was not with her; he had left a soldier named Gaspard in command of the escort; which slept, it appears, in Moulins ; among the soldiers was Duprat, the paid spy of the Count—a villain my cousin would not have lodged or fed. She says it is possible that these two may be tracking my lord Duke, while the lady travels slowly to Lyons, but she has no certainty; only your lordship's wisdom can solve this riddle."

"I must think," Rolland said. "It is late, and night brings counsel along with sleep. Waken our fellows at daybreak, and wait for me with them on the further side of the town." Mathieu sat talking with his cousin, the hostess of Le Cur Loyal. When night fell, he went into the town. He was far more definite next morning respecting the route they ought , to follow in pursuit of the Countess. He did not speak till they were out of Moulins, and then he asked if my lord Vicomte knew that the Constable had fled to Chantelle, and had left it a few days later.

"I was not fully sure," Rolland said. "Are you certain that your cousin's news may be trusted? A woman, you know, is seldom accurate in the way she repeats what she hears. " Mathieu smiled. "I am married, my lord. My cousin Th6rese is honest, and speaks the truth, but I do not depend on her only. I have friends in Moulins, and last night I had speech with two; I may not name them; if I could do so, my lord would be satisfied. They tell me that the Count de Laval—or, as they call him here, the Chevalier de Retz—was seen in talk with one Gilles Duprat, a discharged servant of my lord the Constable; they were watched, and next morning this fellow rode off with Monsieur de Retz, before the Countess and rest of the escort passed through Moulins. There seems to be no doubt that de Retz and his men are tracking the Duke, and in that case they are bound for Le Puy, in the Auvergne." "But what would the Constable be doing in the Auvergne? Between Lisieux and Laval I gathered that he was levying troops so as to make head against any force which the King might send to arrest him."

--Mathieu shrugged his shoulders. "Ah, my lord, he is wise and powerful • I cannot understand it. His strength lies here, where he is known and loved and trusted, where everyone but a traitor would shed the last drop of blood to up- hold his cause against the Regent, for my lord the Constable has no quarrel with the King. My lord will not wish to lose an hour, or I would have asked him to see these friends of the Duke. They say that he will cross the Italian frontier after he has traversed Savoy, and that he will hold a com- mand in the Italian army." "He has then, probably, left France? I crave my lord's pardon; the Duke must cross the Rhone at Vienne; and while the army is at Lyons, I learn that the river is jealously guarded some way up and down stream; it is thought that his highness for the present will lie concealed in some of the little villages of the neighbourhood, where he is not known, but where, if recognised, he would never be betrayed." !' Rolland rode on, biting his lip. It seemed ex- tremely probable that Laval had gone in pursuit of the Constable, but it was puzzling that he should take Jeanne along with him. At last he said abruptly over his shoulder to Mathieu: "Ride up close; I want to ask you a question: You said yesterday that when you were in Italy with my lord the Duke of Bourbon the Chevalier de Retz was one of the officers of his staff. Was the Chevalier in favour with his Highness ? " "Yes, my lord, he was so till after the first skirmish; and many of us, who saw and heard things which so noble a prince would not stoop to become aware of, wondered, while we held our peace. It was, as I said, some days after the first skirmish; the Duke was riding by a village to see Monsieur de Pomperant who, had been wounded. Only Lao and I were riding a short way behind him, for Lao had come to fetch him to see his friend. Flying out from a door in the stone wall of a garden came a girl—her feet seemed scarcely to touch the ground till she flung herself down on the , road in front of the Duke's horse. If the beast

had not been perfectly trained it would have reared, and some mischance 'would have befallen the girl; but the Duke soothed and quieted it, though it snorted and trembled with terror. Before he could speak, Lao and I had seen a dark face look out from the gate, the face of the Chevalier de Retz. My lord Duke bent forward, and looked kindly at the girl. who still knelt before him. "` Rise, mademoiselle,' he said in Italian—we used to say he had a kindly feeling for the people, seeing that his lady mother came of Italian blood—' it is not seemly that you should kneel to me, and you terrify my horse. If you have a boon to ask, be kind enough to let me hear it.' My lord knows the royal dignity with which he speaks, and the gentleness that tempers it. Tell me, mademoiselle, how I can help you. You have nothing to fear.' My lord, I can never forget the despair in that girl's eyes as she looked over her ehoulder at the gate. Then, seeing no one—for the Chevalier disappeared as suddenly as he came—she told her story. Now that she stood up we could see that she was very tall, and she had, I fancy, been beautiful, but her eyes were swollen with weeping, and one cheek was purple as from a heavy blow. She grew very white while she spoke; it seemed to Inc that she had a hard trial to keep herself from sobs and tears. She said that she was an orphan, her father had been a Milanese officer and her mother's relations were noble, but poor; as the French troops entered Milan, De Retz had seen her at a window: she was nursing her dying mother. He had somehow found admission to the house, and had gained the good- will of her father. Her mother died, her father was killed by a chance shot; De Retz professed ardent love for her, and proposed marriage instead of the convent, which seemed to be her only refuge. She Consented, but one delay after another came in the way, till she was suddenly informed by the owner of the house in which her parents had lived that he could no longer harbour her, and that she had sacrificed her reputation by receiving the visits of a Frenchman. She therefore became the mistress of De Retz, on the promise that he would marry her when the war was over. She had followed him disguised as a page, but lately he had taken a dis- like to her, and bade her leave him; to-day, when she refused to go away, he struck her, and at last he bade her remain, and told her he was going to turn her over to one of his soldiers, named Gaspard, man he knew she had an especial dislike for. It was to ask protection from this last outrage that she had determined to seek the Duke, when she learnt from the gardener of the villa where De Retz had placed her that the Constable was even then passing the garden wall. "My lord, I do not know what became of the lady, but on our return the Constable sent for De Beta, and saw him alone in his tent. "They came out together, De Retz like a whipped hound, though there was black fury in his eyes. The Constable's look was terrible. I said to Lao that his eyes reminded me of a lightning flash. He bowed to the Chevalier, and said: Let it be done to-morrow at latest.' We knew afterwards that he had made De Retz promise to marry the poor lady —Francesca was her narne2—but next day De [lets asserted that she was nowhere to be found. At this my lord Constable was so angry that he told De Bets out before witnesses he was no longer under his banner. My lord will know whether the Count of Laval, as lie now is, can bear much love to the Duke de Bourbon. My informants at Moulins said boldly that he was seeking the Con- stable that he might deliver him up to the King and earn the price that is set on his head." "We are as far to seek as ever," Rolland said abruptly, "unless, indeed, one can glean tidings at the inns on the road."

„My lord, craving your pardon, I fancy the Chevalier will not need to go to Le Puy; were I” —he looked round him to be sure no one else was within earshot—"if I, my lord, were seeking this fugitive, I should go only a little south of St. Etienne; there or thereabouts we shall hear of the Count and our lady."

CAMBRIA TIMM:TOM • CAMERA.—This is the title of a delightful boiklet published by the Cambrian Railways Company, and descriptive of the choicest scenery in North and South Wales. The views are, without ex- ception, exceedingly pretty, and not only creditable to the photographer, but to the engraver and printer as well. "Cambria through a Camera,"—the very title calls to mind innumerable fairy glens and places pictur- gigue which abound in Wild Wales. In addition to the pictorial excellencies of the booklet, there is a most in. teresting context from the facile pen of "Lesser Colum- bus," who toured over the Cambrian line in company with th• General Manager Mr. C. S. Denniss. We need hardly remind our readers that all these places of beauty illustrated in the booklet are most easily acoess- ible by the Cambrian line, which itself passes through magnificent mountain eabaary.

div.head: CHAPTER XVI. TILE MOUNTAIN TARN.
div.p: CHAPTER XVI. TILE MOUNTAIN TARN.

Yet, after all, Etienne de Retz, now Count de Laval, had gone to Le Puy. He had almost a certainty of finding the Constable in the volcanic region around it, but he thought it unwise to encumber himself with Jeanne and her women. He had therefore directed the leader of her escort to wait for him at St. Veriol, a village near St. Etienne; he was so sure of capturing the Constable that he had deter- mined to take St. Feriol on his way to Lyons. Jeanne would witness his triumph and would be induced to receive him as her affianced hus- band. He did not fully trust her; he had nd faith in women, he knew that most women had romantic ideas about the Constable, who, though he had never been, ,a squire of dames, held chivalrous principles as to their treatment; he had good reason to know that, he told himself. If Jeanne were to guess the purpose of his journey, she would probably side with the Duke; more than that, she might be capable of warning him, for she- seemed to Laval to have a rare spirit for her years. He halted at Yssingaux, and was told by a surly Swiss soldier that the Constable had been recognised the-:.day before, not far from Le Puy. Besides Gaspard, De Retz had about a dozen soldiers with him; almost all of them were able to recognise the fugitive should he be met with; so, although they had ridden far and fast, and horses and men were well-nigh exhausted, their leader insisted on pushing on to Le Puy. On their way they passed a lake, or tarn, which, half-way up a lofty hill, filled the crater of an extinct volcano. It was not far from the by-road; they had taken a shorter way, the Swiss told them, than the high road; and as De Retz observed the tarn he also noted a figure beside it, which shewed in bold relief against the grey rock that rose behind the water.

Laval rode on till his troop was out of sight of the stationary figure; then he called a halt, and bidding Gaspard and the rest wait for him behind a huge boulder that projected into the path, he dismounted and followed a narrow goat track cumbered with ashes and scorim ; the track led, as he expected, after a few detours, to the lonely tarn. The figure he had noted was a man of middle- height, clad in green, a well-worn wallet hanging from his girdle, into which he was diving with both hands when the Count came up. "Good evening, friend," said Laval. "Mort Dieu I are fish to be found so near the road ? "

The stranger wore long hair, and an unusual amount of beard. He slightly frowned as he put esp his hand to enforce silence. "Thou my friend art more of a disturber than the passers-by," he said very softly. "What matters it about the number of fishes? I come here for sport, not for supper, else an empty belly would often be my portion." Laval stared. "I thought the sport consisted in taking the fish," he said. "What, then, have you in your wallet ? " The angler slowly pulled out a wriggling worm, and then a small bottle in which was a live minnow. "And you have taken naught ? " The man looked up at him through his tangled hair.

"Parelieu ! must it be only the catch that com- pensates? Is there no pleasure in the chase? It must be so, or why am I here? Day after day I rise with no such intent, and yet ere nightfall I find myself beside this bit of water." He looked at his rod, which he had laid aside, and then at the track by which the stranger had approached him, as if to intimate that he desired to be alone. "Yours is a strange occupation in such stirring times, when every strong arm is needed for the King's service." Laval spoke scornfully, and the stranger sighed. "My arm is no longer strong," he said sadly; "a blight has fallen on it. Let us talk of other matters; thou dost but tempt me to repine when thou speakest of serving, the King." "Well, then, friend '—Laval had delayed his question for fear of betraying eagerness—" 7-3 you spend your days here, you must note passers-by on the way below. Have you noted any to-day or yesterday? " "If I did not think thou wert one of them, I could say a dozen or more of horsemen passed but a while ago, on tlieir way to Le Puy, I reckon, and yesterday two horsemen went by in the con- trary direction." "Say von so ? " Laval's eyes glittered, though he spoke calmly. "I expect to meet friends here; one is very tall and has a distinguished appear- ance; the other is—well, much of your own height and aspect." The angler smiled. "Those may be the friends thou seekest, for as they passed by I noted that one of the horsemen was of noble bearing, and taller than his fellow, who was in truth ordinary as any burgess; but thou hast pro- bably met both these cavaliers near Yssambaut." Laval put a restraint on his joy. "The very men! but we met no one—no one; those cavaliers may have followed the high road, which they could turn into about half an hour from this, for though this way eaves distance, it is olaguev rough for the horses."

The. angler did not answer; ms eyes were MN on his line. ravel had not done with him. "Are you from Le Pay?" he said. The angler nodded. "Then you can tell me how the town is affected. I mean, whoher it stands by the Bing, or by the Duke of Bourbon ? " The angler half-raised the flapping hat that shadowed his face. 1 "Vies is roil I trow we are King's men in Le Puy; and, stranger, I counsel thee to keep a quiet tongue in thy head if thou art, as I guess, in favour of the Constable." "I, Mort .Dieu !—I am bound for Lyons, where the rest of my levy awaits me; yet I have served under the Duke in old days, and though I deplore his present course, on my faith I would not betray him, should such a chance fall in my way; on the contrary, I should advise him to return to his allegiance." "And you think he would listen? Mort Dim! it has ever been told in my hearing that Charles de Bourbon is not to be moved from the way he has once chosen; when he has really chosen it he is set like a rock. For my part, I lack belief in his treasonable intentions towards the Bing." Laval looked keenly at the bearded face. "On our road here," he said slowly, "I halted at Moulins, for I was puzzled by the news I had heard further north. The tidings I gathered at Moulins left no doubt of the Duke's treason." "This interests ma What didst hear at Moulins ? "

' The angler's tone of lazy indifference lulled Laval's rising suspicion; he had begun to think that this fellow might be the Constable's spy. Now he saw that his first impression had been correct, and that this was one of those besotted fools of whom he had heard, whose world was limited by their sport, and who took little interest in aught outside it. "I heard at Moulins that though the lord Con- stable was ill in bed, so ill that he could not even rise to greet his Majesty, yet soon after his Majesty's departure he was in the saddle, and on his 'way to La Palisse ; he went thence to Chantelles —he, the sick man, who was to travel slowly in a litter to join the King at Lyons." The angler looked surprised. "Ville le roif Say you so? Well, well, they should know the truth in the Duke's own city; yet he may have gone to Chantelles but to raise troops, and has, mayhap, joined the King from thence. What think you?" ' Laval turned impatiently away. "Mort flicut all the world knows that the Duke I left Chantelles days ago; he is said to be near Le Puy; He intends to pass into Savoy, so as to join Pescara in Italy." "Does the wind blow that way ? " "Stay? ..;, Thou hast at last told me something I had not heard before. Hast more news stowed away in thy doublet ? " He called this out loudly, for Laval was hurry- - ing away. He waved his band, and was soon lost to sight among the grey crags. The angler stayed a good half-hour beside the tarn; he did not hook a fish in the interval; then he rose, and with his long rod on his shoulder, began to circle round the high rocks that rose behind the water. He found himself in a sort of basin, around which the tall grey crags, fantastic in form, clustered as if they were guarding a secret; between two of them was a dark blot, the entrance to a cavern in the rock. The angler stretched out hierocl, and tapped three times on the rock just above the opening. Out of this came, after a while, a bending figure, wrapped in a cloak that concealed him. Seeing only the angler, he stood erect, shewing that he was very tall and of commanding aspect. His broad hat shadowed his face, which was of almost ivory tint, with jet-black hair and beard; his eyes, as he turned them inquiringly to his companion, were very black and brilliant. "Was it he? "

The angler bent his head, and related the news which Laval had brought from Moulins. "My lord will agree that it is useless to return to Le Puy." "Call me Friend John; it is simpler and wiser; and I will call you Friend Peter. I will go back to my first idea and make for St. Bonnet; it is so miserable a place that no one will seek me, and Tarbes is faithful unto death: thence the passage of the Rhone will be easy. You think this fellow is tracking us? " "Why else is he here? He professes friendship; but his eyes belie him; I have put him off tb,e scent,, but, Foy de via vie! I for one, shall fech safer when the Rhone is between us." "We must move quietly," his tall compailioll said. "I have a friend at the Fleur de Lys, ilea',, St. Etienne, besides one at St. Bonnet, where no one Would think of looking for us; but we must reach the hostel before this dog leaves Le Puy." (To be continued.)

Four sappers of the Royal Engineers' time- expired men have, I learn, been engaged to go out with Mr. Mohun's expedition which is to construct the telegraph line from Lake Tanganyika to Stanley Falls, in the Congo Independent State. The men have agreed to serve for two years, and they will be paid £2OO a year each. Tee chief engiceer. Mr. Thornton, and Dr. Castellore, the medical officer, also an Englishman, who served witn Sir Teubman Goldie in the recent operations on the River Niger, sail from Antwerp on the 20th for Zsneibar, to obtain porters and donkeys. The project as at first planned was to carry a telegraph line from Tows, on the west shore of Lake Tanganyika, in a north- ixeNterly direction to Karonga, en the River Congo, a distance of about 200 miles. It is now, I learn, proposed to continue the wire down the river for abuut 400 miles to Stanley Falls, thus bringing that suition, in the very centre of Africa, into tele- graphic communication with Lendon by way of Lake Tanganyika and Mr. Rhodes's trans-continental lice. All the material for the telegraph, med:cal stores, &c., have been obtaintd in this coantry, and their transport, via Chin a, Lake Nyassa, and the Stevenson road to Tanganyika has been arranged for with the English African Lakes Steam Corpora- tkm.

Mr. Curzon's acceptance of the Viceroyalty and the resignation of his seat in Parliament does not necessarily •acate his Foreign Under Secretaryship. After a rest at Reigate he may. therefore, be ex- pected to return to the Foreign Office to carry on as huainess, at all events until Lerd Salisbury le- turns from the Continent,when Mr. Curzon's succes- rior will probably be appointed. The arrangement will, howe•er. depend on Mr. Ourzon's health. 4i He emancipated as speedily as pos- sibleuties at the Foreign Office, in order twe 0 puel arpborot ae ing some of the more immediately pressing problems with wh ch the Indian Govern- ment has at present to deal—such, for example, !as the Ut hriestit beingd y currency queqien, a problem with which Mr. Curzon is only imperfectly acquainted. ! Mr. Curzon was not Lord George Hamilton's first ' choice for the office of 'Viceroy, a, the polition was °affotr:nddtodeclined Lord Balfour of Burleigh a month or two , on the ground of Lady Balfour's bgesitu. There is no member wheFe reputation has Parliament so conspicioitsly within the last vriesaerli noirtwo as Mr. Curzon's. It would have been - higher if he bad been more gracious in manner and more civil to hie questioners, who, as he generally gowere discharging a lawful duty. But the rise of his reputation owes much to the import- ance and number of the questions with which the Foreign Office has had to deal. Hie subordinate poaition has prevented him from being responsible I. for Jard Salisbury's failures, but, he has defended h ilws.ith great ability and complete elLt mias dsteePar ryorde

Sir John Lubbock's memorial on the subject of the eorly closing of shops has been handed to Mr. Balfour. The document which bears the names of more than two hundred members of Parliament, representing all shades of political opinion, urges upon the Government the necessity of supporting in the next session the Shops (Early Closing)Bill,or 80M9 other meroure that would remedy the evil of excessively long hours of labour in shops. The me- morial is supported by Sir Walter Forster, Sir William Priestley, and Dr. Farquharson on medical fl rounds; by Messrs. Burt,Burns, Fonwick,tibraham, Arch,and Broadhurst as working-men representa- tives; and by lealing Conservatives and Liberal Unionists,as well as by Liberals and Nationalists.

The heat wave which is passing over us is causing a great number of deaths by sunstroka and heat apop!exy in London. It appears to be in Lowlon where the heat maximum ha+ been reached, at least, I have seen no provincial record which chron- icles so high a temp.rature as has beers experienred in tile metropolis. Yet,at the meteorological office, the heat is only regamie i as normal summer heat. Less than ten days ago everybody was complaining of the cold weather. The evenings were chilly and more than once showed signs of frost. Thee we were plunged rapidly, without warning, into the resent grilling atmosphere. On got:day the ther- mometer stood here at is highest summer figure,as yet. basing reached 90 degrees in the shade during the afternoon.

Public attention has of late been so much ab- sorbed in railway concession questions in North China that the substantial progress of the only Bri- tish railway approaching the Chike,e frontier has wearied observation. Quite recently orders have beau given for what is known as the Gokteik Gorge Viaduct on the railway from Mandalay north eastward to Kunlon on the Salween, which is to be one of the largest viaducts of the kind in the world. It lies forty miles beyond Maymyo,and the bridge is to be erected at a considerable height above the stream,and it will be 2,110 feet in length. It will be a steel structure of ten spans of over 200 feet each. It is approached by two tunnels with an aggregate length of 1.760 feet, and the whole length of the section of which the tunnels and via- duct forms part is to be seven and a half miles.l Three years are to be given to the work, the con- struction of the line in the other sections proceed- ing meanwhile.

Tee defects in the French naval service dis- covered and publicly announced by M.Lockroy, the new Minister of Marine, were, 1 have reason to be- lieve, already well within the knowledge of the British Admiralty, whose agents keep them well in- formed as to the condition of the French navy. XL Lockroy is supposed to be the writer who more than a year ago, under the signature of " Three Stars." contributed to the " Revue de Pai is " some striking articles in which the 'very defects which he has now officially exoosed were stated to exist. Tt is said also that M. Lockroy is at the bottom of an attempt to found in France an institution simi- lar in aims and operations to the Navy Laague here.

There is consternation among the dwellers in the great Peabody Buildings, the trustees—among whom are the Duke of Devonshire and Mr. Walter L3ng, M.P.—having . resolved to raise the rents all round. How large is the population affected may be eEtimated from the fact that the buildings con- tain 11,367 rooms, all of which are occupied. If there were ten times more they would probably be tensir.ed, so great is the demand for them. When for example, the trustees opened 146 sets of rooms in Bedfordsbury they had 2,500 applications for them. The average rent of a room is 2s 2d, of a "dwelling "—which means two, three, or four rooms-4s 9.d: while the mean weekly earnings of the occupying families are .£1 33 21c1. What are the causes of the rent raising ? Higher rates and more exacting sanitation. The phrase " philan- thropy and per cent " used to be taken as repre- senting Mr. Peabody's view, but the buildings only yield 20 per cent. There will, however, be only small additions to the rents ; and as the profit is Tent on more buildings the new move may pro- mote the happiness of the greatest number.

--- All interested in the promotion of a feeling of friendship with America are deeply concerned at' the possible transference of Colonel Hay from the American Embassy here to Washington. He has rendered splendid service to the cause which aims at binding the two countries in a closer alliance. But as a member of Mr. M'Einley's Cabinet he should be able to do more to cement the relations of the two countries, at Washington, than he can even in London. Since his arrival in England he has become immensely popular in Society 'circles, and his return to the States will be regarded here as a serious loss both politically and socially. All that can be wished is that his snccessor will be animated by a desire to keep the future relations of the two countries on the same footing, and from what is known of the feelings which prevail at the White House we may expect in Colonel Hay's suc- cessor a man of like mind with himself.

div.head: BOATING DISASTER ON LAKE DER,WENTWAT &R. A NEWTON MAN'S EXPERIENCE.
div.p: THE BOATING DISASTER ON LAKE DER,WENTWAT &R. A NEWTON MAN'S EXPERIENCE.

The inquest on the bodies of the five young women who were drowned by the loaed iring of a hat on Like Derwentwater on Friday morning was held on Satur- day morning at Keswicic, before Mr. Gordon Falcon, the 'West Cuaaberland coroner. The names of the dece teed were Mary Alice Smill (21),Nancy Pickles (20), Frances Crossley (21), Helena Clegg (21), and Mary Jane Smith (21). All of the deceased were weavers, employed at Nelson, and were friends of cue another, and were also I members of the National Home Reading Holiday I Association. The vessel, which was drawn up on the shore of Crow Park for inspect.o 3 by the jury, is a strong looking craft,2ot long, 41t. beam, and 18in. deep and before it was sold to its present owner was used at ithe Keswick landings, being registered to carry six persons. Mr. J. Broatch, solicitor, appeared onbehalf of the National Home Hemline Holivay A several of the relatives of the deceeelsciattioa and of !o ci John James, outfitter, Regent-- Ci e rcus, Swindon, said he went with the two riser, Line and Ratcliffe and the deceased ladies to the landing on Portinscale side. Three boats had gone. Radcliffe asked tee boatman how many the boat would take. He replied eight. Seven had already got in the boat, and Ratcliffe got in, in addition. They started abeut 9.35, and the ladies we-e grouped in the stern. Witness rowed the bow and Lane the stroke oar. Radcliffe was in the bow of the both. At commencing the water was comp tratiyeny calm. The further they went the worse the water b .came. They pulled ahead of all the boate.and then fell second. Some one cried across to them" Will the geetleman " (mean- ing Radcliffe) "sit further in the boat." Radcliffe said, "I don't evi,h to grt wet," and get up to move. Witireee told him to it down till told to move. Ono of the girls at the back began to move, and Eiadcliffe passed along Ithe boat. Radcliffe sit in the boey of tie boat inrtie midst or the ladies. We had paesed the first ieland,con- tinued the witness, and the waves were terraely high. My intention was to get on the lee of the island and get to Keswick. The girls behaved bravely Miss Clegg was steering under the direction of witness and Lane. A few minutee after I heard a shout from one of the ladies, " Heigh! stop." I saw a lunceeon b isket floating away, and a lady's arm held towersis it. I stopped rowing, an was about tri " he clr water " %ghee someone cried " The boat is tilling." Tue bolt beean to sink before we could do anythiag. I called to L tee, " Unship oars and throw to the ladies." Lane failed, but I managed to throw mine. I called out to the girls " Catch hold of the oars and boat." It was terrihly rough, and as! plunged in the water I was knocked nearly insensible by a wave. On comine to the surfa •e, I tried to swim towards where the boat was submerged An oar was near, and I pushed it to ialiss Crossley, hut I was dashed under again. Whea I came up she was still there with the oar near her, but she failed to grasp it. I was again dashed under. On rising I saw no ladies, but Radcliffe and Lana were clinging to the boat, which had come to the surface. I get an oar, which I .put under any right arm, and struck out with the left. By a desperate effort I got another oar. I trod the water and in a few minutes heard a noise, and saw a beet 30 or 40 yards away. I saw ladies and hats in the distance. I called to the occupants of the boat to save the ladies, but none were to be seen. Thee two men in the boat picked me up. By the Coroner: Witness thought Radcliffe moving to the back must have put too much weight at the stern. —By Mr. Broatch : He had real the Union rules of boating as to overcrowding. Ile thought they referred to promiscuous and not organised boating. John Henry Lane, Newton-le-Willows, printer, agreed , with the previous witness as to the boatman's statement ' as tie its capability to hold eight persons. When some- body called to Radcliffe—" Get farther back and the boat will go easier," witness said " You had bett,r be careful," After that Radcliffe moved down in fr tnt of witeees to the centre of the boat. Witness rowed till the boat began to sink. He did not hear anyone say there was a satehel lest. Seeing water in the bottom of the boat, he remarked that the boat was leaking, and the girls said " Yes, our feet are wet." A moment later th y said" The water is coming over the sides." The boat Seen afterwards moved over, and threw all into the water. He sank a little, and as be ro,e he felt someone grass his Eft arm and put a hand upon his right shoulder. Finding that the weight was dragging him under, he struggled to get his left arm free. As he came to the Surface he was still held—he thought by one of the girls. The boat wan about five yards off, bottom , upwards- As the girl had left hold of him he sciz id the keel of the beat, and tried t 3 get upon it, bat it hee'ed over and he fell back into the water. Swimming ' again to it he put his right band on the keel. One of the girls rose with the back of her head to the boat. Ile put his left hand under her chin, and held her head agiinst the boat for some time, but it heeled over again, and he was driven off. While he had hold of till girl, a beat came round. Somebody made a grab at her but missed her. He thought James was being rescued. The water washed him from the boat, and when he got back to it the girl had disappeared. He got astride the boat and lay down. Ratcliffe was at the other end. Witless cried to Mr. Small "1 am all right." They took Rad- cliffs off, and afterwards witness got int 3 the boat. He I had been accustomed to boating on the lake at Newton-I le-Willows,and he understood the menagement fairly well He did not think it alto tether wise for Radcliffe to move, but as he was ordered to do so from the ether boat wit- case opt:Weeded it was right. The bows of other boats were quite as high out of the water as theirs. Replying to jurymen, witness said he thought there was too mule weight on the stern. After hearing other evidence the jury retired, and were absent 40 minutes. Their verdict was handed to the Coroner. They were of opinion that while the de- ceased had been accidentally drowned the b oatman had committed an error of judgment in allowing eight per- sons to go in the boat. At the same time they were of opinion that if the boat had remained trimmed as at the start the accident would nct have occurred. They also thought that the number of passengers to be carried should be registered on all boats let for hire, as at Kes- wick.

div.head: AN AMERICANS IMPRESSIONS OF MANCHESTER, WARRINGTON AND LIVERPOOL.
div.p: AN AMERICANS IMPRESSIONS OF MANCHESTER, WARRINGTON AND LIVERPOOL.

-An American who evidently knows how to use his eyes contributes to the New York Evening Post "some notes on what he has seen in Liverpool, Manchester, Leeds, and Glasgow. He has,in parti- cular, been struck by the great increase of popula- lation in industrial Lancashire and Yorkshire since he went over the same ground six years alp " Within the next twenty years," he thinks. " Liverpool and Manchester will be hyphened Vo- -1 gether by a continuous series of towns," He 1 touches a weak point when he comes to our tram- ' cars. To one accustomed to tha electric cars that run in all the great and many of the smaller towns in the United States it must be amazing that we should lag so tar behind. " Here in Manchester," he cbserves, " the street cars are still hauled by horses, and in the densely populated region extending or twenty miles round Manchester there is, so far as I have observed, not a single electric car." Nor can an American fail to be sur- prised by tie cumbrous and ugly Aaiun tramcars that do duty in some of the Lancashire towns Leeds has made a start with the electric cars, and Liverpool and Manchester will soon follow suit. Even then there will be plenty of le"-way to make up, in all conscience. " Warrington," this taker of ;notes among us c.bserves, "is. in fact, cs free from streetcars as it was a century ago,although within ten miles from its market hall there must be a ! population of 200,000."—" Manchester Guardian."
THE SHOCKING FATALITY TO A. RAILWAY EMPLOYE AT WARRINGTON.
THE CAUSE-A FAULTY COUPLING.

An inquiry concerning the death of John -William Green (32) of 42, Longford-street, Warrington, em- ployed as a boiler washer by the London and North Wes- tern Railway Company, whom shocking death we recor- ded last week, was held at the Police Station on Mouthy evening. The deceased leaves a widow and five children. . _ .

The loremax of the jury was Mr. John Harrison. Mr. F. R Roberts appeared for the relatives of the deceased, and Mr. Bland for Vie Company. There were also pre- sent Inspector Rogers (El. M.'s Government Impactor), Mr. Starkey (station-master at Bank Quay), Mr. Mar- shall (locomotive superintendent)._

Th 9 first witaess called was Henry Green, 19. Now. road, Latchford, who said the deceased was his brother. He was 32 years of age last birthday. Witness last saw him alive about a month ago. He saw the dead body on Saturday. John Burke, 13, DI ller-street, Latchford, a foreman shunter on the Louden and North Western Railway , stated that when he cams on duty at two o'clock on Friday afternoon, the foreman who was going off duty gave him instructions as to how the sidings stood. Ho told witness that there were three sidings in which he must not shunt waggons as they were fouled by a crane which was lifting a disabled waggon into another waggon for removal. The three sidings mentioned as being occupied were toe Pteston, North, and back road. Witness then proseeded with the shuntine of a freight train comprising 38 waggene. He gave the pointsmen orders to turn the points for the shed siding, number' 1, and Earlegown. Witness superintended the shunting and he placed one waggon in the seel siding, and had succeeded in placing three others in number one siding 11 when he gave the driver the signal to stop, in order tol prepare for the shunting of ;:soine waggons into the Earleatown siding.No sooner had the driver brought the train to a standstill then he saw to lois surprise that fifteen waggons had broken loose from the train and were travelling into the Earleatown siding. He afterwards found that the waggons broke away in coaseqaeace of a link of the coupling giving way. Witaesa did not know at the time teat the Eerles- town siding was fouled by the crane, and even if the waggons had not brakea away of themselves he would have put some of them into that siding, but be would have got the train to shunt slowly and would not have interfered with the crane. There were already a number of waggons in the Esrlestown siding, and it was these that struck the crane when the waggons entered the siding. The Coroner, by means of an ocular densonstratien with a number of cooks showed the jury how the shunt. inc operations were conducted. He stated that the rail- way coin/eau:es Inan were doing 1 eeitimate work, when by some means tee link, which was now produced in enurt. gave way and caused the waggons to run into the ' E ,rlestown siding. The broken link having been handed to the jury for examination, Mr. Daintith said it was badly flawed. The Coroner: Tae point is weather that fact could have been found oue by previous inspection. Mr. Jeffrey (another juryman) said that an inspection by the eye would not reveal the defect, nor would sound convey the def ,ct to the ear. Inspector Rogers (to witness) : How long are the coupline chains allowed to be worked without being ex- amined? Witness replied that he could not answer that ques- tion. Inspector Rogers : Are the coupling chains ever taken off or replaced ? Witness : I cannot answer that. It is not in my de- partment. By Mr. Roberts: There were four lines or rails which were fouled by the crane. He was only aware of three at the time. No flagman was on duty at the time. Re could not say whether the three lines should have been padlocked. He was acquainted with the rules of the company,he could not tell them whether the lines should be padlocked or not. Re knew rule 109 which related to the use of cranes. The witness was asked whether fixed signals were used on this line, but he did not reply. The Coroner (after reading the rules twice): A lawyer must have drawn this up. it is so obscure. (Laughter.) Having read the rule to the jury, Mr. Brighouse asked Mr. Roberts if he understood it,and the latter replied that he was trying to do so, but that ho was relying on rule B. Mr. Roberts (to witness): Ate there any fixed signals on the siding? Witness : Na, sir ; not fixed. The Coroner: If there had been a flagman would that have prevented the accident ? Mr. Roberts : No, sir, but I understand the lines should have been so locked that the waggons could not have got on to them. Mr. Roberts (to witnrso : Is there such a cust 3m as to padlock the lines that are being used in this way. Witness : I cannot answer that. This is the first Cala I have bad a crane in my yard. It was not my duty to padlock the line, I was only third foreman. The Coroner: But if you had been the first foreman with a corresponding increase of Wages—laughter— would you have used the padlock? Witness : If I bad been in charge I should have seen that everything was secure before I started to work. Mr. Bland : With the exception of a royal train, or where we have a rail out, is it customary to padlock a line as suggested ? Witness : I cannot answer that question. Mr. Bland: If the waggons had not broken away and you had gone on with your shunting into the Esrlestown eiaing,should you have had sufficient coatrol over them to prevent them coming into contact with those lying on the same line ? Witness: Yes. sir. The Coroner: The accident has happened through the link breaking. Mr. Bland: Does the waggon belong to the Lyndon and Norlh-Weetern Railway Company? Witness : No, sir. Mr. Bland : As a matter of fact was the broken link attached to a Ltanddu mineral waggon ? Witness: Yes: The Coroner: It is a foreigner—% Welsher in fact. (Laughter.) Mr. Bland : Is it your °Pinion that if the link had not broken you could have put the waggons in ? Witness : Yee. The Coroner : We have only to see whether some woe has been so negligent that we ought to send him for trial. To my mind the matter is quite clear, and the accident has come about through a brokea link. Mr. Jeffrey (a juror) : That is quite evident. The Coroner: Why should we labour the thing ? Let another tenant thrash out who is liable, there is no fault of the signalman, engine driver, or foreman shun- ter. The accident is owing to some inherent defect, some latent defect in the link of a foreign waggon. - Mr. Partingtem, (another juror): No one in the world, in my opinion, could have prevented the aleid ant. The Coroner : Let the parties tight it out elsewlyr as to whether anyone is responsible for the defective link. _ -

William Shaw, 19, Dickenson stre crane driver, said•,t he was the driver of the crane hi question when the accident happened. Tile: wers hoisting the damaqed waggon into a carr,ago. It was a hand crane. While at work a ccrtain nuumber of waggons dashed into thp ballast box. Witness said to his mats " I wonder if anyone is hurt ?" He was the first to find the deceased underneath the wagerm. Ha could not tell how the °Ton ha l fallen, i but t must have fallen to the

I think there is sufficient evidence before you to enable you to come to a deAsion._ _
The Foreman : Ido not think there is any diuty about the matter.__

The Coroner: If you like you can retire into the magistrate's room tc discuss the matter in private. The jury then retired to tli magistrates room and when they returned the foreman announced that the jury had agreed upon their verdict, and it was that a sheer accident had occurred esti ;ed by a faulty coupl- ing.

TEMPERANCE ELECTORAL PATRIOTIC UNION. There was the election and installation of officers I of the Temperance Electoral Patriotic Union, Eng- land's first fort No. 1, at the weekly meeting held on Friday last week. There was a large attendance. The officers elected were installed by Brother J. C. Morton, Supreme Chief Patriot. They were :—Bro. Steel, C.P. ; Brother Brandreth, V.C.P. ; Brother Ilaigh, chaplain; Sisters Templeton and Brayshaw, armour bearers ; Brother Brandreth, secretary pre tern; Brother Lister,assistant secretary; Brother Bluck, usher; Sister Allen, assistant usher ; Brother Molineaux, sentinel; and Brother Simister, guard.— Brother Steel in a short address, thanked the mem- bers for having re-elected him to the post of chief. —Brother Morton also spoke of the able manner in which Bro. Steel had held the post for the last three quarters. The programme consisted of songs by Sisters Templeton, Morgan and Jolley, and recita- tions by Bros. Morton and Steel. Brother John Naylor was unanimously elected hon. chief patriot.

Tea was provided by Mr. Brough at the farmhouse of Mr. Charles Johnson about half an hour later. A. visit was subsequently paid to the church and mere, and the party who were joined by some visitors from Manchester, spent a very pleasant evening. The return journey was commenced at eight o'clock,and Warrington was reached about ten o'clock, an en- joyable day having been spent.—The members of St. James' Church Choir, Latchford, numbering 27, accompanied by the Vicar (the Rev.
