MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL COMPANY.
HALF-YEARLY MEETING.
IMPROVED PROSPECTS.

Last Thursday the -t-ev.eiTy-;i/Ct-ti--ot:dir;:r.y general meet- ing of the shareholders of the Manchester Ship Canal Company was held in the Association Hall, Peter-street, Manchester, Mr. J. K. Bytiaell (chairman of the board of directors) presiding. There was a very large attendance of shareholders. Among those present were Earl Egerton of Tette°, the Lord Mayor of Manchester, tee Mayor of Salford, Alderman Sir Bosclim T. Leech, Sir Joseph Leigh, Alderman Sir William 11 Bailey,Alderman Southern, Alderman M'Deugall, and Mr. A. H. Whit- worth (secretary). The Hon. R. Reid, ex-Minister of Victoria, Australia, occupied a seat on the platform. The report and statement of acceunts were taken as read : They are as folio we : The report of the directors of the Manchester Ship Canal Company for the half-year ended June 30th states that the net outlay on capital account was £17,052. The total expenditure on capital account amounted to £15,179,224. The Seip Canal revenue receipts amounted to £106,695, and the expenditure to £86,122, leaving a credit of £20,573. The profits of the Bridgewater de- partment amounted to £21,706. The balance carried to net revenue account was £42,279, to which was added £3,970 for bankers' interest, making a total credit for the half-year of £42,669. The amount standing to the debit of the net revenue account was £707,035. Interest for the half-year on the first and second mortgage debentures amounting to £44,742 had been paid out of the net revenue and the accumulated revenue of the Bridgewater department. The interest due to the Man- chester Corporation, £112,500, was net paid, and tiee total amount owing to the Corporation now is £731,250. The net revenue from the Ship Canal portion of the undertaking amounted to £20,573 as compared with a loss of £894 on the corresponding period of 1897. The improvement was caused by increased earnings and re- duced expenditure. The toll-paying merchandise passed over the Ship Canal during the half year reached 1,173,880 tons as compared with 957,210 tons in the first half of 1897. Seaborne traffic showed an increase of 196,712 tons, mostly in low-class articles. Coal which yielded little revenue, showed an increase of 90,000 tone. Grain imports showed an increase of , 21,400 tons, and the tank oil trade had made a rood beginning, 20,300 t3n3 having been imported, although the installation was not completed. High rates of freight interfered with the timber imports, and floods in Spain caused a serious falling off in the fruit traffic. Timber was 11,000 tons less than last year. Frieglets having now declined to a much lower level, timber chartering had been resumed, and it was hoped that during the latter half of this year the imports of timber would be very large. The Chairman, in moving their adoption, said the statement they were again able to submit to the share- holders showed substantial progress. In support of that statement he would have to trouble them with a few figures. The weight of seaborne merchandise dealt with on the Ship Canal during the last half of last year was 783,000 tens. During the year just concluded the weight was 980,000 tons, an increase or 197,000 tons. The result of the working of the Ship Canal department of the first half of last year was a debit belanoe of £894, but this year they had a credit balance of £20,573. (Applause). The profits of the Bridgewater Canal last year were £20,017 ; this year they were £21,706. Taking the whole of the net revenue, including a small amount of beak interest, they found that last year the total was £19,671. They, therefore, had to take £25,071 from the accumulated Bridgewater revenue in order to pay interest on the first and second debentures. It might be , interesting to compare the whole of the year which ended June, 1897, with the year ended June, 1898. During the year ended June, 1897, the total net revenue was £51,037 ; during ihe year just concluded in June last it was £84,277. Therefore the improvement for the year ending in June last was £33,240 of net ' revenue. (Applause.) He did not like to prophesy ' before he knew, but he might state that his opinion was that the current half year would enable them to pay £44,743 first and second debenture interest, and recoup the smell amount of £2,073 which they were short this heir year, and some thing more (hear, hear). He would be oisappointed, in fact, if the year 1898, taken as a whole, did not enable them to pay £89,846 which became due on the first and second debentures, and also pay a small amount to the Manchester Corporation. The measure of that hope for improvement would be be t illustrated by saying that the year 1897 resulted in their beina short of £28,207 to I meet intereet on the first and second debentures. They l would leave been able to pay the Manehest( r Corporation a small amount this balf.year had it not been that their usual great stand by—he meant timber— had to a great extent failed them temporarily. There was, in the spring of the year, just whoa the timber shippers made their charters, a great boom in freights, which advanced to something like 40 to 50 per cent., with the result that the charterers held off, and shipments of timber to this country were small during the first half of the year. They had, therefore, to meet a decreaee instead of their usual increase. There had been a coueiderable falliag off in the imports of green fruit in consequence of the disastrous floods in Spain having des troyed a large portion of the craps. The question might then be asked how was it that they got 197,000 tons Increase of seaborne traffic. They had an increase of 90,000 tone in the coal exports, and of 11,800 tons in the exports of textiles, whilst among the imports they had an increase of 21.000 tons of grain, 9,000 tons of cotton, and others. This large increase in the weight of merchandise handled on the canal only resulted in an increase of £9.400, because the largest augmentation was in low-class traffic,which paid only a small toll. In the railway and labour department at the docks there bad been an important saving. They had now increased and improved appliances at the docks. They had to some extent been aseiste 1 by trio more reasenable attitude assumed by importers. It was Cheer- ing te find that they were on eve of giving something in the shape Of interest to the citrzons of Manchester. (Applause.) It was nct unreasonable to hope that that tact would stimulate them not omy to give therie teeir I own traffic, but to use their influence to get more traffic. (Applans Proceediog.the chairman referred at length to the traffic progreesmrel prospects of the undertaking, I and compared the trade now carried on with that , of the last several years. Owing to the coal strike in Ssuth Wales, he said, the coal in Lancashire had by meaus of the canal, been introduced iim now markets. They hoped that coma when the strike was over they would see a permanent increase, and that steamers coining there to discharge goods would load with coal at Partington. With regard to the timber trade, freights were novo lower, and chartering was brisk. The directors were anxiously watching, their tim- ber imports, and it was to be hoped that during the 'latter half of this year the imports of timber would be 'large. They believed that the new grain elevator would enable them to obtain a largely-increased trade in this ceminodity. Cotton during the seasen jest ended showed a substantial increase, and with anything like aesietauce from the spinners they would have a further increaFe during the coming reason. They would have sailings from a large number of American ports. Very much depended upon the at- titude of the spinners if the trade in cottan was to in crease. If they were determinded that cotton should come to Manchester,and not to Liverpooathere would be a large increase indeed. They had also every reason to believe that during the coming winter they would hive a very large trade in tank oil. Upon timber, grain,, CettOnsParer materials, and tank oil depended ad =Me- diate increase of their revenue,and lie appealed to those who had influence to help forward BIWA trades. They had Nat lost sight, however, for a moment of all the other trados,and they would not slacken their efforts to obtain them and retain them. For a considerable time they were endeavouring to form a steamship company with the object of placing lir ze, powerful modern steamers on the Manchester sera co—that wee to sey, to run only to aid from Manchester. Trois hed now been brought to a satiffeetory eonclu?ion. The 7 0570,1 a ereat deal to their friend, Sir Christopher Furness, in tne neater. It was the beginning of a movement which would eventualla enable Manchester to rank as a first-class shipping port commensurate with the ina,gnitede of her waterway and her docks (applause.) The Manchester liners had a large fleet on the stocks leuildioa, In time meantime, they had put two steamers on, and Sir Christopher leurness had put to steamers on on his own account. The Chairman referred to a visit paid by Sir Bosdin Leech and Alderman Southern to Canada order to promote trade between that colony and Man- chester, and added that the visit of these gentlemen had been very successful Oae reason why they were so very thankful to have the Manchester liners established was that they had now Every prospect of a continued supply of cattle to the (mirages on which Itlanchester had spent so much maney to beeefit the undertaking. Impel t ant servioe had been rendered by the firms en- gaged in the coasting trade. They still had to. deplore, with the exception of Bombay and the Petsian Gulf, that they had none of th 3 export trade to the east of the Suez Canal. The original promoters. of the under- taking were largely influencoe by the Idea of helping the cotton trade. It eves one of the .ltiest amnia' spectacles of the present day thafi while shipowners combined effectually and dictated payment of shipments and rates of freight and every other condition, the mer- chants, who paid the freight, had not been euecessful in making any combination te deal with the shipowners on equal terms. American manufactured cotton goods were DOW going from New York to China and Japan at lees than half the rate of freight that was paid from Birken- head to the two countries he had named. Yet they were surprised that the cotton trade was not quite as as r, ought to be ! flourishing 'Thee hoped for nreat things in tern I from tire Isr ze works. IThe Chairman proceeded Co speak of the developmf met ot traffic het es Manchester docks,. The Alkali Union were making rengememits to convert some old works into ( works ter the making of phosphate manures, and as the phosphates would have to, be imported this would lead to a large .onount of traffic. He lookel upon the gradual development of large trades on the banks of the canal as important and ealesfactory ; for it would be imooesible to work a treffie at the decks at this etri sufficient t

pay a dividend on the whole of the capital. The whole canal must in time be utilised as one long dock. (Hear. hear.) He also mentioned, in dealing with this Part of the subject,the four large tank oil installations,the Man- chester Corporation lairages.Mesirs. Richard Evans and Co.'s coal depot at Acton Grange, the Partington coal port,the Wholesale Co-operative Society's Soap Works, the Warrington lay-by, the Runcorn lay-byes ; and, in course of coestruction, the Colonial Produce Company's large cold air stires at Mode Wheel and the Patent Fug Wcrks in Trafford Park. Many other negotiations were pending, but it was not possible to say when any of them would mature. The development of the Trafford Park Esiate was,he understood, pro;ressing, and would no doubt eventually bring a great deal of traffic te the canal. He did not want the shareholders to take too rosy a view of the immediate foture,but of the ultimato success of the undertaking there was no doubt whatever, (Applause.) He concluded by moving the adoptioa cf tae .report.

Alderman Southern, in s3conding the metion, said it was the most satisfactory half-yearly report they had yet received. Mr. Isherwood asked how it was the Australian and Nt3W Zealand traffic which was boomed some time ago, was either dying out or beimg suppressed, or boycotted, or whatever they liked to term it. He had had some information furmshed to him which tended to show that. Australian and New Zealand people hal not had fair treatment.

The Chairman, in reply, said the reason lay with the Confcrence or shipping ring.inastauch as they would not allow shipowners who were even willing to send goods to Manchester to do so ei.ccept upon terms that would I not ensure their getting a cargo. The Australian Premiers were iu Manchester last year, and they went over the collat, together with the Canadian Premier. All those matters were laid before them, and all that was possible was being done to get thar opinion upon them and have a better state of things brougat about. Mr. Isher wood said there WAS also a good opening in Manebester for the development of the tr ade in !rather. The Coairman replied teat since the establishment el the Canadian service th 1, hal had a moderate accession of traffic in I,at ier and a good many promises. The trade had not been overlooked. Mr. Gueit asked whether the through rates question was finally settled....

Th. C ilircnan said that their manager had had an in- terview with the railway managers, and although a few rates still remained to be settled, their manager assured him that he thought, within a very short time, every- thing would te arranged. Their relations with the railway companies, he was happy to say, were at the present time most amicabh, and they seace,d to be desirous of making all reasmable arranagementa.— (Maar, hear.) . _

The motio•n for the adoption of the report was then put and carried unanimously. The Coairman moved that the best thanks of the meeting be tr.ndered to Mclennan J. W. Soutnern and Sir Bosdin Leech for their eminent eervic sin C triads, in bringing about the benefits which, he was sure, would accrue to the Company therefrom. He felt the meeting was entirely with him, and be thought it a ould be a graceful thing if they were to ask them t 3 accept a small honorarium in return for having given up their own business engagements for several weeks in order to pro- ceed t 3 Canada in the inteeeats of the Canal Csmpeny. If they were to offer them £250 it would, he was sure,be- in accordance sal' le the wishee of the shareholders, and a very fitting thing to do. He therefore included the proposal in his proposition. A shareholder having seconded the motion, the motion was than put and carried unanimously. Mr. Aldermen Southern slid he was extremely proud at receiving such a vote. Ile had told Mr. Bethell that if there was a single dissentient neither Sir sdin Leech nor he wi,uld accept anything. The Hon. R. Reid, (an exeniniater of Victoria) who was heartily received, said it was a great pleasure deed to hint to answer one or two of the pertinent questions which he had heard put to the meeting regard- ing the failure of the trade with his part of the British Empire. It did seem to him to be a great mistake that after having spent so many millions in bringing within reach of Manche iter all tha trade and traffic of the British Empire it should be shut out by the manipulations of a cleverly managed and engineered shipping nog. (Ap- plause.) He commented on the fact that ail the wool sent from Australia to England was shipped to London, whereas the Port of Manchester had York ihire, which was the great market for wool, at its very next donr,and he could uot understand why importers should be con- tent to pay the carriage from Landon to Yorkshire. Were they, he asked, going to allow the revenue of that great enterorise of others to remain stagnant for ever for want of combination against abs skipping ring? They mutt not think for a moment that they had got a soft thing on,"—(Laughter.) The members of the I shipping ring were just as hard headed as were the men of Lancashire, but he was sure they only wanted to know the facts and understand them fairly and the remedy would net be far off.—(Hear, hear.) The Chairman said as the matter had been broached, he took the opportunity of saying that there was only one remedy. They bad on the on, hand shipowners in effective combination not swerving in the slightest de- gree,and they had no combination to meet it. Every in- dividual shipper was dealt with separately, and how, then, could they expect that ship owners would not dic- tate their own terms? The remedy of the thippers must be that they should not be dealt with individually, but sllou!d 131 in a position to maxis their own bargain with the aid of combination. That was what the Hindoo Mer- chants in Bombay bad don," with reference to cotton, and now those merchants, to the number of 290, made their contracts every two years, and got a very low rate of freight. The trade in Manchester had te -writ sd in consequence.

-- At the close of the business, art extraurdicafiv_ twetin was held, at which, on the motion of the Chairman, semnded by Mr. Alderman Southern, the shareholders atsthorised the directurs,in p srsuauce of the Manchester Ship Canal Art. 1897, to hurruw any sum or sums not exceeding £lOO.OOO on the sectirity of the Company's surplus lands, subject to the consent of the Corm:ll.2.lOn of Manchester, in accordance with the provision' of the above-mentioned Ac. The cunsent of the Corporation had been given to the buirowin; of the sum of £50,000 in the meantime.

div.head: SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO ALDERIEIN
div.p: SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO ALDERIEIN
FRA.NCOMB.

We regret to hear that Alderman Francomb, J.P., C.C., met with a serious accident whilst return- ing from the Mare and Foal Show at Walton Park on Thursday last week. In company with Alderman Hutchinson and Councillor bee he was journeying in an open carriage to his residence at Wilderspool, and wtren coming through Stockton Heath by some means or other he was suddenly thrown out of the conveyance and fell heavily to the ground. His injuries were such as to deem it advisable to call ia medical assistance. D. Parker made an examina- tion and found that tha Alderman had sustained severs iij uries to the ribs two of which were broken. Under the cars of Dr. Parker he is progressing as favourably as can be expected.

A tragic affair resulting in the death of a young man named Rodger. Is reported from Lune, county Antrim. It is alleged that deceased was out poaching on Sunday !sight on the lands of Mr. William Maine, along with a friend, when his gm acoldentidly went off, the contents lodging In his right lung. Death was instantaneous.

SPAIN knows the na, Spain and Her Losses. of the concessions she have to make to and the wonder of the situation is that the is regarded with indifference amounting to ap Cuba will go, through responsibility for the will remain. Porto Rico will go, and the
iture will
Amen'
.._ Laa-

rones, and the capital of the Philippines. few of the islands Spain has failed to rule success fully will remain under her control. The con' traction of the empire will be considerable, and ought, we should think, to have cast a gloom ova the whole country. At present there is a stupct that indicates the existence of a considerable previous strain, which has now passed away. Th. country will gradually become sensible of the losses sustained. But will they amount to se much in substance and reality as ie generally supposed? We doubt it, and fc't several weighty reasans. The burden of mailr taming authority in Cuba has been a greo and constant drain on the resources of Spain. '4 fleet has had to be maintained, and a larger aria than sufficed for the defence of the Peninsuler' merely to keep down tho rebellious spirits in tbe Pearl of the Antilles. This expenditure will noWf cease. With it will terminate also the cost ° sending officials to the island, who merely dered it for their own personal advantage. I:211er tions of money owing and spent apart, the probe' bility is that Spain will be better off than she was before, more especially as there is no war in- demnity to pay. The adventurous Dons vvill 115" to pay attention to home politics. The people will hardly feel a less which ineY be ac- companied by a diminished call for soldiers Or foreign service. The fact is that Spain's islantli Possessions have not been real colonies. No one migrated to them from Spain. They were no out: let for a surplus population. No families ever wel° out to them to live or to engage in commerce; They—were possessions that provided careers Of aristocrats, and that was all. The same state °f things was not uncommon in the early history ° some of our own Colonies, and it has not who° passed away in our West Indian Islands. 111,e real value of such colonies is always doubtful' Commercial considerations do net seem to 138/11 had much influence. Spain sent few of her mitotz' factures to these islands, and other countrie° reaped quite as much advantage as Spain did the way of extra commercial busiaess. When tbe whole case comes to be summed up, therefore, loss will not be very extensive. It may be sentimental than financial or commercial. The old barbarian element is strong in us all. The love of sport with the gun is a bit of our ancestry coming out, breaking asunder the layers Of propriety and respectability which have been keeping it down, century after century. The t3n- 46ncy of townsfolk to want to go out in a boat When they get to the waterside is another bit of Primitive life, impossible to wholly suppress. Now, We should be sorry to see this adventurous 97irit crushed. It is the secret of empire, of colonial de- Velopment. It has given us our sea power,and we cannot afford to lose that. I-, was ENIMMON who laid that any British Minister is ready to take the -Command of the Channel Fut. If we pay for our • tlualities in the shaoa en a a.;I: dls it hardly seems as if it could be helped. Where one adventure terminates fat al:y. t'loi.%) fi,Z*3 th msands that come oft all right and give pleasure. Still, adventure is always the better for having its spirit 'tempered with knowledge and prudence.

The Hooley case has been aptly described as an application to commercial affairs of the Policy o f the Double Shuffle with which a certain C.mtin- 'arta' diplomatist was wont to bewilder his an- tagonists. On Lilo whole, Mr. Justice Wright's Interpretation of one of the side issues of this be- Vildering case will cornmeal itself to most people, though there are many who will still think that Earl De La Warr escapes mercifully when he is described as "indiscreet." It is true that Lord De La Warr has been acquitted of any imputation of Influencing Mr. Hooley to give false evidence, but he has not yet cleared himself of all the unpleas- ant inferences that naturally spring out of the ad- Mission that he received certain sums of money from the fallen financier when h e became a direc- tor of that financier's companies. This is the point to be borne in mind : did Earl Do La Warr and the other noblemen who accepted directorates receive money for becoming directors or not P They deny it. Mr. Hooley, on the other hand, still maintains it. And it is significant that Mr. Justice Wright for his part will not say that Mr. Rooley is an indiscriminate liar,though he appears to believe that some cf the facts of the case have become encrusted with imagination in their pas- sage through Mr. Hoeley's not very clear brain. Attempts have been made to apologise for the acs tiett of those noblemen who accepted money i4rPra Mr. Hooley, but the public will agree with ;Lir. dward Fry that whenever a man receives any- for making a recommendation or exercising 4'4l,Zuence he is bound in honesty to disclose it to anis person he is endeavouring to influence.

Amid all the pomp and magnificence of the übilee Naval Review the eyes of the experts were on the towering ironclads, or the beautiful lines of the swift cruisers, or the long black hulls 4sf the deadly torpedo-boats, but upon a little Vessel rushing hither and thither at the terrific Speed of over forty miles an hour. To them the Turbinia opened up a vista of accelerated Service tremendous tremendous in its possibilities. The genius of man is gradually annihilating space, but the in- i vontion of Mr. Parsons will shortly lead to de- velopments so astonishing that had anyone Prophesied their realisation a few years ago he Weald have been openly derided. It is now calcu- lated that if an Atlantic liner is supplied with tl.gines like the Turbinia's the journey across to "t:Tw York can be accomplished in three days, "41ch is less than half the time taken by the latest Cunarder. But on the Mediterranean,where C°aling stations are numerous, even more remark- results are attainable. Steamers can be built With a speed of over fifty miles an hour. It is impossible to say where this revolution of marine motive power will end. The speed of the express train can be equalled for a brief period even at the present time. But the supreme difficulty which has yet to be surmounted is the question of coal. The consumption of coal by the new engines is simply enormous. Fortunately the engines are exceedingly simple in construction, and occupy considerably less space than the present propelling Power. But this economy of space will not ade- quately meet the huge increase in coal consump- tion, and it is to be hoped that Mr. Parsons will be successful in his endeavours to overcome these Practical difficulties.

By fining Jane Johnson on Monday morning the Warrington magistratei prevented her from ful- filling her laudable intention of exterminating the inhabitants of Silver-square. Long have the denizensof this district been a source of trouble to the police, to whom and the town generally it would be a great boon if Silver-square could be re- reeved from the map of Warrington—as Mr. T. Birchen recently remarked. Now Jane Johnson, Who has the reputation of being a woman of her Word in these matters, vowed she was going to screw round the necks of all the people in Silver- square. And as,literally,it is the people more than t„.lle locality who are the source of mischief,we think 4ane ought to have been allowed to pose as a phil- 44thropist to this extent. She is admittedly the .1131 person fitted for carrying out this simple plan "( extermination, and it does seem a pity that her !tell-meant intentions for the Silver-square inhab- itants should have been so rudely nipped in the

Warington traders to whom, even now, the ship Canal is a boon, will regret the decision of the company in respect to their request for the Privilege of egress at Runcorn lock. The directors Of the company looked at the matter from a point of view which if it had been aqticipated, none the less furnishes them with good grounds for refusing the. concession. Moreover they will probably be relieved of their obligation to construct the pen- stock, and without giving Warrington any quid pro quo. Perhaps the Corporation are hoping for future favours. At any rate their policy of graciousness is far preferable to dog-in-the manger dealings with the Company, and will, very probably bear good fruit in the end.

Sankey Brook still "stinks in the nostrils of men," but according to Alderman Roberts twelve or eighteen months will see the elimination of the foul deposit which has been the source of trouble all these years. He again explained the position of the St. Helens Corporation and emphasised the fact that the present evil must be remedied before St. Helens could think of carrying out their BeYeme for connecting a water-carriage system ,ith the Brook. The only thing to be regretted la that the means of attaining the desired end necessitate such a long delay.

div.head: PATHETIC CASE AT WIDNES.
div.p: A PATHETIC CASE AT WIDNES.

Considerable excitement was created in Widnes on Saturday by the news that a man, supposed at the time to be an escaped lunatic from Rainhill Asylum.had beel seen wandering about the fields adjacent to Milton-road. Information was lodged with Sergeant Bennett at the Police Station,who immediately despatched a number of policemen to search for the supposed lunatic. The offi- cers discovered the man in a nude condition running through some standing wheat. They gave chase, and P.C.Scott succeeded in effecting a capture.A waggonette happened to be at hand,and the man was placed in this and conveyed to the Police Station. Here it was ascer- tained that the man's name was James Walker,a joiner, residing at Dittos. It appears that Waiker, who is a respectable man,has lately beea in a very depressed con- dition owing to hi inability t, follow his employment on account of his failing eyesight. He was afterwards banded over to the Relieving Officer. PRESENTATION TO THS REV. H. C. MOYLE.

On Friday evening a meeting was held in St. Mic.hael's Church vestry for the purpose of making a presentation to the Rev. H. C. Movie, when there were present Mr. J. H. Weston (preiidine), Revs. H. C. Moyle, H. B, Firth,Scholes,and o,ive^,Mrs.Alfred Lighthurn and Miss Vriswall, Messrs. W Moller, Alfred Lightburn, M. L. ' Davies, J. Shorlock, Gordwell, Douglas, Youd, Hobson, J. Littler, Clark, Cook, Rowles.—Mr. Weston in present- ing a beautiful silver pocket Communion service to Mr. Moyle said they wore all aware that their friend was about to take leave of them and enter unon duties at Efarsham, and whilst wishing. him "God speed" in his new field of labour, they felt they could not let him go without showing in some slight manner their apprecia- tion of his good work and their kindly feeling towards him ; therefore he would ask Mr. Moyle to accent as a small token of esteem from the people of St. Michael's that pocket Communion service. Mr. W,ston then c tiled upon Mr. Mellor to complete the presentation. Mr. Mellor upon rising said he had very great pleasure in handing to Mr. Moyle a purse of gold. He hoped he and also Mrs and Miss Moyle would he vary happy in their new home and that they would enjoy good health.— Messrs. Lightlourn, Davies, Littler, and the Rev. H. B. Firth also spoke.—Mr. Moyle very feelingly responded to the warmly expressed good wishes.—On Sunday evening the Rev. H. C. Moyle preached his farewell ser- mon to a large congregation at St. Michael's Church, flan, the wer Is "Finally brethren farewell; be perfect ; be of good comfort; be of one mind; live in peace, and the Gad of love and peace shall be with you."

div.head: RUNCORN' FREE LIBRA.RY COMMITTEE.
div.p: RUNCORN' FREE LIBRA.RY COMMITTEE.
THE ANNUAL REPORT.-OPENING OF THE
EXTENSION.

On Tuesday evening, Mr. Daniel Bisbrown presided over the Library Committee which sat in the Council Chamber,at the Town Hall. There were also present-- Messrs. W. jzfamkinqun, W. Handley, M. L. Davies, Joseph Pritchard, and Mr. J. D. Jooes (librarian and secretary). During the month the Library had been open for the issue of books for 15 days. during which time 1,072 volumes were issued, being a decrease of 160 on the car- responding period of last year, embracint; the following subjects :—T .eology, 10 : philosophy. 4 ; science, 33 ; history, etc., 36 ; poetry, 7 ; fiction, 830 ; music, 7 ; mis- cellaneous, 145. The Librarian submitted the 16 h annual report of the Library Cemmittee. The number of borrowers tickets issued during the year was 711. being a decrease of nine as compared with last year. The Library had been open 240 days,and 21,968 books were issued, being a decrease of 977. The average daily issue was 92. There kad been added to the Library during the year 198 volumes, of which 161 were purchased, and 35 presented ; which brought the total up to 8,700 volumes. The valuable bequest of the late Jr. S. Beckett Chadwick, of between two and three thousand volumes, and a large number of cases of natural history specimens, necessitated the extension of the Library premises before they could be accommodated. The Urban District Council were approached, and a plan prepared by their Surveyor was approved. The extension provides a general reat3ing room with spacious entrance from Egerton-strset, and the present reading ro)ms will be used as book stores and reference reading noms. It is expected that the extensions will meet the requirement of the Library for some years to come. The Committee again express their thanks to the various donors of money, books, periodi- cals and newspapers. Mr. Handley proposed the adoption of the rep art. Mr. Hankinson seconded, and it was unanimously agreed to. The Librarian reported the receipt of the following gifts :—From the Co-operative Union Limited,"Thirtieth annual Report of Congress, 1898 " ; from It stherhithe Free Library, report. With regard t 3 the openisg of the extension,there was a general opinion that someone should be asked to come and formally open it. and upon the motion of Mr. Hankinsontreconded by Mr. Davies, it was decided to invite Sir John Brunner, to perform tho cere- mony, No special date was fix d ; but the beginning of October WAS mentionei as the most likely time.

A CHILD KNOCKED DOWN BY A BICYCLE. As a little lad named Robert spencer, three years of age,and living at 4,Wharf-street with its parents, was attempting to cross Wharf-st. about six o'clock on Monday night, a cyclist, named James Smith,ls, General-street, came riding up from the direction of Bridge Foot. The cyclist rang the bell and the little child,instead of going straight on,turned back in his confusion and was knocked down and his skull fractured. The child was removed to the In- firmary in an unconscious condition,but by Tuesday morning it bad recovered consciousness.

div.head: EX A MINER FRIDAY, AUGUST 19, Ig9B
div.p: THE EX A MINER FRIDAY, AUGUST 19, Ig9B
SAVAGE ASSAULT UPON THE POLICE AT RUNCORN.
A COWARDLY CROWD.

On Tuesday night,High-street,Runcorn,in the vicinity of the " Eaaminer" office, was the scene of a savage assault upon the police, which occurred when Police- constables Gregory and Bowyer, who had bsen called to eject some men from the Holyhead Harbour Inn, (kept by Mr. Henry Decorte) vrsra executing their duty. One of the men Tucker struck the coustables and Licensee. The constab'es then attempted to arrest the man, when two or three more became involved in the affray, and for a considerable time the street was in an uproar. And it was not until assistance had been obtained that the police succeeded in locking up tlie'r assailants. _ .

On Wednesday morning before Messrs. F. J. Norman and Julio Ockleston,at the pol ce court, which was held in the magistrates, owing to the court-room being in course of extensive alteratioo,and to which large crowds tried to obtain admission but failed, William Tucker, a seafaring man ; Thomas Burke, sailor ; William Booth, labourer, Nelson-street ; and Sameel Woods, compositor, were brought up on several charges :—Tucker, charged with using obscene language,and assaulting police Con- stables Gregory and Bowyer, whilst in the execution of their duty in High-street on the previous night, pleaded guilty ; saying he remembered something of the kind but was " mad drink" at the time.—Burke, charged with assaulting the two officers at the same time and Place,pleaded not guilty.—William Booth, charged with obstructing the police. pleaded guilty.—Samuel Woods, , charged with a like offence to that committed by Booth, pleaded not guilty,alleging that if anything he assisted the police, as he put the officer's helmet on. Police-Constable Gregory gave evidence as to being on duty in Devonshire Square, on the Tuesday night, ab Jut 7.15 p.m. in company with P.C. Bo wyrr, who WaS tell- ing him about three men that he had been called neon to eject from the Holyhead Harbour. Just as he was speaking the men passed. Two of them were Tucker and Burke, but the other one was not atom hend: d. Fie saw the three men go to the W,,terloo Bridge, where they stood fo a little while, after which they returned and proceeded back again to the Holyhead Harbour. As the men went in Mr. Decode, the landlord, came out in his shirt sleeves. They (the constables) went down and the men came out. After coming out the three men were standing together, when thpy toll them t 3 go away. Tucker said he "would knock witness's face in" using the obscene language alleged. Bowyer asked him to go away and he said be would not go for 40 police men. He then said "if you don't go away we will lock you up." Tucker then struck him,after which they attempted to lock him up. They succeeded in getting him as far as the "Examiner Office" where they took shelt ni in the porch. On account of the violence of the prisoner. B fwyer got out his handcuffs to put them on Tucker. Prisoner knocked Bowyer over and snatched the handcuffs off him hitting witness on the forehead with them. Be also struck both of them several timos,as well as alr. D.,cer ie (who was trying to assist them). Prisoner was shouting and cursing at the top of his voice all the time. On coming outside the " Examiner Office " he struck Con- stable Bowyer off his legs into the road, and struck witness many times in the face. They taen got him as tar as Lea's Temperance floteLand eventually to the Police Station; finally having to handcuff him and tie his legs, as well as strap him to the ambulance be fore they succeeded.—The prisoner Burke came to the assistance of Tucker, and assaulted both officers in the IPorch of the " Examiner " Office. He tried to rescue the man at the same time saying" Let him go you b— swine."—William Booth put his arm round Tucker and tried to drag him away, which caused Tucker, who was then quiet, to ge off again into a violent struggle. Be also used very bad language and cried " give it the b—s."—Woods tried to get the man away by Bel- amy's shop, and witness told him to" go away or he would ba in the Fame place." Woods was apprehended afterwards be P.C. Smith. Cross-examined by Mr. Linaker ; He had never had any difficulty with Mr. Decorte, and considered that the Holyhead Harbour was a well conducted house. Police-Constable Bowyer corroborated the preceeding witness, adding that he saw the men first at 7 p.m., and turned them out of the Holyhead Harbour. There was a crowd of something like several hundred people in the Streets at the time of the assault. He considered that the men were not drunk, although they had had same drink.

Cross-examined ley S. Woods : He admitted it was a fact that someone put his helmet upon his head, but he could not say that it was Woods. Mr. Henry Decorte, licensee of the Holyhead Harbour, gave evidence of a corroborative nsture, adding that when Tucker first came he went behind the bar and threatened to break the glasses. fie did not serve-thems not because they were drunk ; but because he did not want them in the house. Tucker also said he would " break the house up." He did not know Tucker at all. Mr. James Lei, proprietor of Lea's Temperance Hole', also corroborated. There was one of his windows smashed during the self& by his place. Dr. Finlay MeDoegal having given evidence of a cor- roborative nature as to the assault upon the police, which he saw, said he wished to take that opportunity of expressing his surprise at the conduct of the crowd in not doing something to assist the two police officers who were doing their duty, and especially as he knew one of them, P.C. Bowyer bae only just recovered from a very severe illness. He was astonished to see the way the officers were treated, and took that opportunity of saying that the crowd ought to be aseamed of them- selves. He was also sorry to obs,rve that these rows were very frequent in High-street, and had been occur- ring for a number of years, and he wished to press upon them the fact that although it was necessary to have somewhere for these sailors to go to—too much surveillance could not be exercised in looking after them. He had taken the trouble to visit the men in the cells and examine them,as they had made serious charges against the police officers, and the result of the examination was to snow that the men had not been treated in the way they stated. With regard to the man Tucker he eould only say that he was "mad drunk" and bad simply lost control of himself, and it was he (witness) tbat suggested to the police to take the man down on the ambulance,so as to save him from him- self. He could only speak in the highest terms of the way—the considerate way, in which the officera treated their prisoners. Called to give evidence for Wood, Dr. McDougal stid that beyond loosing control of his tongue he did not think that that young man did any real harm.—By Superintendent Okell : He did not assist them, how- ever. Mr. A. Timing, assistant at Mr. Bellamy's,testifie I to seeing Woods with a police officer's helmet,which he put on the officer's heal. He nxt saw Woods rush into the the crowd, which Dr. Mc Dougal was keeping back, and tell Gregory "not to kneel upon the man's stomach, as he was killing him."—ln answer to the Bench, witness said he did not see Woods take hold of the prisoner. The Bench after a brief retirement, returned into court, and the Chairman said : Tucker your only de- fence is that you have been drunk, which is no defence at all. We consider that it was a very brutal assault upon the police, and if others are not prepared to pro. tect them, we are. For using obscene language you will be fined 10s. and 17s. 101. costs or 14 days; for the brutal assault on Gregory you will have four menthe, and for assaulting P.C.Bewyer 1 month,the sentences to run consecutively.—Burke you will go to jail for 14 days for each case of assault.—Booth will be fined 403. and costs, or 14 days.—Acidreseieg Woods the Chairman said that they bad considered his case and would give him the benefit of the doubt.—He (the speaker) was sorry to hear of the town beine, in an uproar and it seemed a great shame for the people of Runcorn to have such things said abeur thorn. He also expr-ssed the hope that the licensee of the Holyhead H srbeur would exercise more vigilance.

div.head: WESTON POINT.
div.p: WESTON POINT.

PARISH MEETING—SCARCITY OF EATEPAYE RS .—On Monday evening a parish meeting was hold in the Church Schools, Weston Point, for the purpose of electiog two representative for the Weaver Ward on the Parish Council. .Weston. At the parish meeting in April last six candidates were nominated for five seats, the full representation of the We tver Ward. Terse of the can- didates afterwards withdrew, leaving two vacancies to be filled no. Before the second parish meeting could be held the County Council had to be approached, and it was in accordance with an order issued by them that the present meeting was convened. At tha time announced for the proceedings to commence only two electors, Mr James Collier (clerk to the Parish Council) and our representative, had put in an appearance. After waiting nearly half-an-hour the two solitary electors and the scribe went forth into the village in search of a few more ratepayers. and at length the attendance was made up to eight, viz : Aessrs. Samuel Savage, James Bisbrown, Thomas Ttaarmes, Joseph Plant, John Plumb, W Johnson, and W Forster. Mr. Savage was voted to the chair, and a very short time sufficed to complete the business.—The nominations were :—George Whitby, 14, Mersey-view, Weston Point, team owner, proposed by James Bisbro vim, and seconded by Samuel Prince. John Griffiths, Cheahyer's-lane, Weston Point, farmer, pro- posed by Samuel Savage, and seconded by William, Johoun.—No oth4r nominations being offered, the Chairman declared these gentlemen duly elected parish councillors for the Weaver Ward. Mr George Comber, and other members of the Cistner Keloer Ambulance Aseociation,were summoned and gave prompt aid ; using attificial respiration voith such good results, that on tho arrival of Dr. Delany, of Runcorn, he highly complimented the ambulance men present, and said that they had done the werk so well tnar there was nothing left for him to do, as the respiration had by that time been complstAy r istored owing t their prompt and skillful treaime et of tie case.

div.p: TtIINCORN NOTES.
[BY A CORRESPONDENT].

For a little time the question of baths is having a a rest. But not for long, as lam given to under- stand that someone who knows is thing or two is now working out a scheme of a tangible, workab'e nature, and talks of pr.lsenting it gratis to the town—l mean the scheme not the baths. What it will be like I cannot yet find out. But this much I have been told, it will be a bath solely to bathe in, and not one for the playing of polo.

The devotees of the game of polo will not like this; and are certain to argue that without polo there will be a greatly reduced incom, which 1 for one am ready to anticipate. Let them argue how they will. We (in Runcorn) want a bathe, a wash, a swim—and for everyone who wants to play polo or see it played, there are about 200 that don't car two pins about it. Having no polo to cater for, a big item of expense is wioed off the sheet.

Dr. McDougal has been talking straight about some of tho public-houses in Higu-street. He in- stanced five of them that were in close proximity to one anoNher —as being far too many for the ons strset. The " rows " in High-street, he said, had well nigh become proverbial. As in all cases the " rowdies" were more or less drunk,to him, the in- ference became obvious. Then, breaking off, he soundly rated the cowar lice of the crowd in not do- ing something to protect the police. This out- spokenne,s on the part of the Doctor is worthy of high commendation, but that Runcornians should merit such things being said of them is deplorable. It is ever the case with torn) people,they do not re- cogrd e the rights of a policeman to be treated like any other human being until one has been killed; then,they suddenly remember that a "policeman's lot is nut a happy one."

Some time ago both our Cycle Clubs were engaged in a battle of words, as to who was going to do the most, or something of the Kind, for the Cycle Parade. Well acts speak louder than words. There are not many of the townspeople who don't know who has done the most, by this time.

The annual report of the Library Commit'ee, be- sides containing the usual statistics,comments very favourably upon the new extension, which it is in- tended to have formally opened by Sir John Brun- ner, NIP., early in October. The new building is rapidly approaching completion, and will prove a vast improvement to the premisEs.

Mr. Frank :ishton's capital innings of 53 not out in the match for Frodsham on Saturday was a highly gratifying performance, throughout which this promising "bat "played in a cool and collec,.ed manner, hitting feeling and giving no chances. The Welsh tour of the Frodsham eleven, especially the visit to Llanfairfechan, provid•id a lot of leather hunting for the Frodshamites, and one would think that their bowlers do not now rate their abilities quite as high. But as a batting eleven the Prod- sham team takes a deal of getting rid of..

In the facs of the controy3rsY which has been flying around with regard to the conversion of a part of the Welsh Coast jut) a second Widnes, the casual observer would regard that town, as the last place on earth for the pursuit of floriculture, but notwithstanding its chemicals, I hear that Mr. W. Farrant, of Widnes, has obtained fourth prize for flower growing from Messrs. Richard Smith and Company, seedsmen andnursery.men,of Worcester, in a competition embracing many thousand com- petitors. This gives the he to those who aver that grass will not grow within two miles of the town, and it is an achievement upon which we heartily congratulate Mr. Farrant.

THE POLLUTION OF RIVERS Mr. Reginald Potte, cle -It to Cheehire County Council, wrote enquiring whether the Rural Council had dealt with all cases of pollution of streams brought under their notice by their inspector of nuisances and all the instances of pollution which wire apt out in the extract from our Medic :1 Officer of Health's report, and whether all such cases had been effectively dealt with and no longer-exist. If there were any cases th t ka 1 not beta dealt with please specify the same The Clerk stated that he had forwarded the letter to their Inspector. Mr Farrington said he had been considering,and found it very difficilt to reply to that matter. If it wes the intention to purify all the streams which were the natural outputs,it would be as undertaking upon which the Council would have to be preparei to spend about half a million of money. Especially if innocuous discol- oration was considered to be pollution. As he had pointed out before it was an easy matter to point out what required remedying, but aoother thing to remedy it, and he should like to see the County Medical Officer try. Mr. Woodward asked did the inspector consider that any of the streams in the district were so polluted as to be injurious to health. Mr. Farrington: No. There are not any like that. Mr. Woodward : Then I suggest that the alswer given to the County Council that they are satisfactory so far as the public health is c ceeerned. If there was no pollution in the etreams at all they would have to close their chief industries. It was Olt nial'ely left to the Inspect cr and Clerk to rely to the County Council's query. TRE ANNUAL CYCLE PARADE.

lOn Wednesday evening, another brick—and a very substantial one was aided to the proposed Runcorn Cottage Hospital, through the exertion of those reap onsible for the cycle pa-Ade ; now an established annual event in the town. The sympathy with the ob- ject of the parade WAS shown in a marked degree on all hoods, and although the " turn-out " was not quite up to that of last year, the response of the public was equally as generous, if not more so. And those respon. irole for the undertaking are to be deservedly congratu- lated upon the success achieved. The procession which was beaded by Suncrintendmt O'kell of she Rumorn Poice), was in the following orcPr :—Marshall, Mr W E Dudley ; Band of the 2nd (E 0) V.B. Cheshire Regiment ; Britsto twins; model of Cottage Hospital:Run _oorn Fire Briga,le;tableao ' "The Sick Child" Victoria Nors ng Guil r;Runcorn Cycle club and local cycl's's; also cyclists from Widnes, Circa- ter, Bowm,n's (Lostock), Warrington, Northwich and ! S:ockton Hah, etc; Widnes Subscription Band ; Black Maria; three men in a boat; two va abonds; trade and advertisement turnauts; theatre art's' es, Drum and Fife bull; Weston ba-id, and a number of comical variety artist s including the "Black (hungry) Band"; the whole being brought up by the Rose Queen" processor from the Rose Ftsival at Weston Point. Toe e t eke ii was through Bridge-stre,t, Chorola street, Lord-street, Waterloo-road, Station-rood, Greenway-road, Victoria— road, Mill Bro Halton-road to crane and hack; having lit up the pro !ession procee&d by way of De.loh Bridge, Bridge-street and High-stree!, to Devonshire Square where a grand finale was given. Toe procession was m irshalled by Messrs. W.E.Dudley,R. Moore,ll. Br inch, 1 and J. Ellison. Throughout the route large crowds lined the through- fares and poured showers of confetti upon both the characters and themselves, and in al incredib'e short time there was nothing to be seen or felt but the multi- coloured confetti papers, and the fun grew fast wad ' furious.

After the parade, a concert was held in the Methodist Free Church schoolroom (kindly lent for the occasion) ;n Greeaway-road, under the presidency of Mr. Samuel Taylor, J.P., C.C., at which Miss Clara Taylor nreseee:ed the prizes won in conaection wite the parade. In his opninte address Mr. raylor sail 'he first item on the programme wag the Chairmau'e address; on would,hewever, assure them that at that time of night he would not make a speech. They had not come to hear a speech from him. He would say thas he was in sympathy, with the object of the eencert, and a more worthy one could not be Obtained. A Cettage Hosp;tal was greatly needed in Runcorn, and great credit was due to those who year by year were workine so zealousy to raise funds to pro- vide one. (Hear, hear.) He had felt its need in Runcorn for some years, and felt sure that it was most gratifying to almost everyone in Runcorn to help forward the fuld, and they wished its promoters every success. A tow years ago the question was taken up, land was obtainer), then come the question of" ways and means," and he was delighted te end that these people were goiug abut it in the right way. (Applause.) There was n 3 doubt but that the question was a very wide one, as many people met with accidents in Rencern, and there WaS no nearer place than Liverpool to which they could be token, so he wished the venture would be so successful as so enable its promoter; to attain their object. (Ap- plause). The following programme wes then gone threugh, the , accompaniments being played by Mrs. Kenyon Divies with pleasing effect :—Song, "Mother's Darling,"M ister Ruttcr (Midget Minstrels) ; Skipping Rope Dance, Miss Edith Jones, (Midget Miastrels); humorous duet the little Misses Kitty Rutter and Fletty tones (Midget Minstrels) ; dance, the little Misses Kitty Rutter and Be te Jones ; coon song, " Is your mereee Mr. Kenyon ; mandoline duett, Mrs. Kenyon Davies and Mss Kenyea ; humorous song, "Oh ! my Bonnet," Miss Edith Jones (Midget Minstr As) ; banjo and piano, Mr. : enyon and Mrs. Kenyon Davies ; clout dancing contest, wo competitors, let. Mr. Huehes ; 2nd, Mr. Conroy ; comic song contost (5 competitors), Ist, Mr. Kenyon, Widnes, " Merry Little Fat Gray Man ;" 2nd. Mr. Lockett," Nothing." The skipping rope dance,and the dance by the Misses Kitty Rutter and Hetty Jones were both excellent items and Were hiehly appreciated. Then followed the presentation of prizes, the names being called out by Mr. F. L. Scott, and the prizes handed to the winners by Miss Clara Taylor. A band of Christie Ministrels, (Messrs. Swett, Harris, Tyrers, and d.. The street collection realised £34 12s. 311., and was made up as follows : coleated by ladies £l5 18s. 91. ; gentlemen £lO 12s. 4t I.; girls £6 3s. 21.; boys £1 18s. THR WORKHOUSE CHAPLAIN. The Rev. L. D. Lyon Bennett. chaplain at the Work- house, wrote sating that he had been very much out of health lately, and a favourable opportunity having occurred for his getting a complete change and rest, he had been only too thankful to avail himself of it. He would be abFeat until September 18th,and had arranged with Rev. J. Llewellyn to act as his substitute.—lt was considered satisfactory. MR. eoyerson's ACCOUNT. Stanley Villas, Runcorn, august 15th, 1898.—T0 the Chairman and Guardians of Runcorn Union. Gentlemen, I herewith nag tohand my account for services rendered in the alteration of your Board-room and building of the lavatory, etc., as per contract, also for the extra work connected with the same, which I hope you will take into consideration. The amount of the original contract was £425, and the total cost has been £573. This work has entailed up in me extra supervision and extra journeys, and as the cost has exceethd the original amount, as above, on that, I have made my charge one third more also.—Mr. Joyns aa's account amouated to £2O, £l5 on original contract, and £5 for extra work.— Tee Chairman said that he committee recommended the payment, which was carried unanimously. THE FURNISHING OF THE BOARDROOM. The Architect, Mr. S. Davies, repaitel that he had paid a special visit to the works of Messrs. Garnett and Soo at Penketh ti inspect the furniture now in course ! of manufacture ter the Boardroom. The tables were in a very forward state and would soon be ready for de- livery. The workmanship was of a high character and ' his drawings were being strictly adhered to. Nothing, however, had been done in the matter of the chairs, and he wished to ask the Board, if it was not too late to consent to an alteration in them, His specification stipulated for the chairs to have upholstered seats • covered with ciro-hide, but Messrs. Garnett subse- quently explained that if they were allowed to make a plainer chair, they would effect a saving of £3O 15i. This offer the Guardians had accept ed. For the sake of £3O 15s. he (Mr. Davies) thought the beard would be better satisfied with the aiphols:ered chairs as specified. However, he left the matter absolutely in tbe'r hands,
and would be glad to carry out their instructions.—lt decided to have the upholstered chairs. THE DECORATION Or THE BOARD ROOM. _

The Chairman reported that the Board Room Com- mittee after due consideration had decided to have the Board room decorated in a plain manner by giving the , woodwork two coats of paint,the mantel-pieces ta be set out in two colours,so as to render the room a little more pleasing, and when it was thoroughly dry it was in- tended to have the room decorated in a thorough manner. Th.l cost,he explained,would be about £lO. He proposed that the recommendation be adopted.—Mr. Mclntyre seconded and the report was unanimously adopted.

div.head: CHILDREN'S FETE AT WESPON POINT.
div.p: CHILDREN'S FETE AT WESPON POINT.
CROWNING THE ROSE QUEEN.-SUCCESSFUL
INAUGURATION.

On Saturday, there was inaugurated at Westm Point, what gives bops of becoming an interesting, amusing, and instructive annual fete. Under the title and style of the" Crowning of the Rose Queen at her own Festival," a very pretly and effective programme was gone . through,in a field (kindly lent by Mr. John Duabayin)at Weston Point, where quite a large number of people from the surrounding districts had assembled to witness I it. Tee proceedings commenced at two o'clock with a precession of Tableaux and numerous characters along South-701(1,0n to Whitchapel,and b ack again. The pro- ceesien was headed by the Salt Union Works Brass Band, and formed a very pretty pseeant as it wended its way through the village streets to the strains of appropriate music. Upoe arrival at the field expositions of the I Morris dance, Rose pole dance, and a presentation of loyal subjects to the Res° Queen were held, each per- forrnance of the children being highly appreciated. About 130 children took part is the affair, and the various costumes and " get-up" throughout were very petty and effective. Tee names of the children 1 arid tee characters they representei are as follows : Queen, Miss M Dunbavin • maids, Misses Lilly Whitby, Elsie Walker, Clara Maddock, Ada Billington, Gertie Dunnavin,Jessie Badman,Sally Gregson; guards, Masters F A.ntrobus, Charles Doris, T Savage, William Plant ; Morris dancers, Misses Blanche Hulse, Lizzie Savage, Jeasie Seine, Ethel Riding, Emily Dodd, Maggie Mus- grave, Lizzie Stevenson, Lucy Latham,E dith Maddock, Eva Whitby,Lizzie Whitby,and Masters John Musgrave, Albert Ham, George Whitby, Fred Riley,Richard Tyldes- ley, Jolla Broady, Edward Johnson, Thomas Riley, James Dele, John Griffith,, and William Maddock ; rose pole dancers, MiSIOS Florrie Walker, Beatrice Boyle, Alias Whitby, Frances Johnson, Jessie Griffi:hs, Ada liebbineton, Mary Jane Rise, Lily Atherton,Amy Savage, Annie ant ibue, Lilly Do Id, Lizzie 'furrier, Cissy Kirk• ham, and fleairc ; ecetlani. Miss Annie Id tl- tm; Ir .land, Miss LIZZIP Whittly ; Wales, Miss Ethel Pritic,e cr rem b•arer, Master E iward Johnson; sceptre beater, Master Geotge Whitby; Spring, Miss Mary Sevege; Semmt,r, Master Harry Musgrave; Autumn, Mess Annie Eaton; Winter, Miss Jessie Myers; flower girls, Misses Maggie Bowden, Emma Stevenson, Alice Keene, and L'zzie Ma.idock ; Lawn Tennis Girls, Misses Ethel Riling, Annie Collins, Emily Cowley, Lucy Wil- kieson -, Grace Darling, Miss Maggie Dunbavin ; Zill- gariciAisses Lizzie Sevenson and Marie Tottell; Babes in the Woo ,Master George ItAckett and Miss Beatrice Beckett ; Ruffians, Masters Fred Riley and Cecil Mills ; Pelicernan, Master Altred Ham ; Gleaners, Misses Louis Eaton,Maegie Johesen, Fussy Johnstm.and L'IV Billing. ton ; Little Red R;dineheo I, Miss Alice Minna ; Grand- mother, MiSS Nellie Burt ; Britannia, Miss Jane An- drews ; Dick Whittington and Cat, Masters Jack Griffiths and John Peach; Little 80-Peep,Miss Lily John- son and Master Fred Walker ; It alien Girls, Misses Lily Savage, Maggie Musgrave, Eva Mealain,and Lilly Abra- bam;Jack and Gi II ,Marite rs Richard Tyldesley and Frank Talbot ; MUSS Girls, Miss Emily Dodd and Miss Sarah Ann Whitby; Skipping Rope Girls,Misses Evelyn Riding, Alice Savage. Fanny Done,and Beatrice Royle;Beauty and the Beast,Miss Gertie Moiers and Master John Musgrave; Fairies (iniluding the good fairy of Weston Point), Misses Hannah Talbot, Flo-rie Beckett, May Beckett, Ruth Lymn, and Alice Watson ; Cinderella and the Prince, Miss Edith Whitby and Master Walter Kirkham ; Old Women that lived in a Shoe, Miss Blanch Hulse ; clowns, Masters William Gibbons and Jobe Musgrave. Afterwards the childr-n sat down to a capital tea, and were provided with ample refreshment. The object of , the festival, which was originated by Mrs Walker and Mrs Broady, was ti provide amusement and a treat for the children of the village. The remainder of the even- ing was spent in dancing on the green, to the strains of the band, the whole concluding with the National Anthem. div.head: MOORE AND DISTRICT HORTICULTITRiL SOCIETY. _
div.p: MOORE AND DISTRICT HORTICULTITRiL SOCIETY. _
FOURTH ANNUAL SHOW.

In Moore Hall Park on Thursday t tie annual show in connection with Moore and Di,trict H3rticul- tura! Society wa held. Since its inauguration four years ago the society has done some excellent work in encouraging horticulture in the discrict, and the exhibits at the show on Thursday were in every way creditable to the exhibitors. The district in- elides Moore, Daresbary, Newton-by-Daresbury, Keckwick, Norton, Higher Walton, Acton Grange and Moss Side. The itev. H. T. Clark is president of the society, and the onerous du-des of vice-presi- dent and hon. treasurer are undertaken by Mr. John White. Mr. Arthur De Feu, is the energetic hon. secretary and the committse is composed of the following gentlemen : Rev. F. W. Wales, Messrs. J. E. Seeker, T. J. Weir, Calder, P. Hamblett, Wil- kinson, Sanderson, Hayward, J. Antrobus, T. Greener, J. Forster,and R. Wilkinson. The exhibits had been • tastefully arranged in two tents, and looked very attractive. With the exception of the exhibits of Mr. Starkey, seed mer- chant, of Warrington, and Messrs. Dickson and Robinson, of Manchester. the whole of the entries were local ones. Amongst those present to witness the opening ceremony wore: Mr. and Mrs. IT. C. Jones (the Elms), Mr, and Mrs. W. C. Jones (the Oaklands), Miss Milner, Mrs. Dennis Milner Miss Groom. Mrs. R. I. Wynne Jones, Itty. H. T. and Mrs. Clark, Rev. F. W. and Mrs. Wale' s Rev. H. and Mrs. Smith (formerly curate of Daresbury, now of Bramborough). Mrs. and Migi Mid beton, Mrs. John Jones, Mr. and Mrs. John White, Mr. J. E and Miss Seeker, and Mr G.B. Adams. The Rev. H. T. Clark in asking Mrs. W. C. Jones, of the Elms, to open the show remarked that it was the fourth annual show, and alt'mugh the en- tries had not been quite so many still the general appearance of the exhibits was the best they had yet had. Fie thought one or two things were worthy of special mention. One wss the table decorations which were very choice. Toe children's ' collection of wild flowers showed a great improve- ment, and with reference to the cottage gardens he could say that they were well wo-th a visit any afternoon. Even if the society had done nothing more than encourage cottage gardening it had justified its existence. Mrs. W. C. Jones in declaring the show open ex- pressed the wish that someone more able had been asked to perform that duty. She was glad to con- gratulate the winners of prizs, and to those .who had not won she could only say" Batter luck next time."

On the proposition of the Rev. F. H. Wales a vote of thanks was accorded the judges for their services. The judges were : Mr. T. Smith Bur- gess (farm produce); Mr. Lockhart,of Walton Hall, and Mr. Parkinson. of Appl toti Hall (flowers). There was a large attendance during the day, and the exhibits were much admired. Messrs. Toogood and Sens, of Southampton offered a silver medal and a bronze medal for com- petition for the best exhibits in the show. The silver medal was won by Sir Richard Brooke, Bert, the bronze medal by Mr. John White, and Mr. Starkey, of Warrington, was awarded a card of msrit. The Walton Band played selections of music during the day.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES,
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES,
HUSBAND AND WIPS.-A WOMAN'S REPRISALS.

_ At the Warrington Boroueh Felice Court on Monday morning, before Mr. F. Monks (in the chair), Alderman Blackhorst, Councillor. Shaw Green and Smethurst, and Messrs. Birchen and Wright, James Graham, 25,Cherley- stret t, was summoned for having on the 91h August and on other dates during the Ist montes neglected his children Amelia (12), .Jame e (8), Matthew (5), and William (one year and fiv 3 men' h 3), in a manner likely to cause injury t) their healtte—lnspecter MacAteer (N.S.P.O C.), whn rrosecuted, seid that about three months aeo the defendant left his wife an, children,who were living in Wes!:-s'reet. and went to live at 25, Cherley-stre t. Derine the titre he had been away he had only contributed sa. towards the maintenance ot the family. The wife an I ti-e children had bees starving, and, in consequence of a steement male by the wife. he (the Inspector) went to the house. He found the children poorly clo' had, and there was no fond in the place except a small p,ecia of a hard loaf and went° , treacle. Be after wards saw defendant ane asked him why be had rot a tended to his wife and family. He said hi a wife was a erunken wman, and he could not and would rot live with her. Be (the InspeAor) asked him why he had not contributed something towards the Children's maintenane.e, and he replied that he bad given his daughter at one time Els., another time fos., and again two half-crowns. For the last 13 weeks, centinued the Inspector, the neighbours had supp-rted the wife and children. T'ae eldest boy, Rot mmtioned in the charge as he was over the age, earned Bs. a week, and out ot ti-at the wife had to pay 44. for r n'. —Annie Woodward, 7, Forshaw-street, said she had fre- quently given food to the childr m. Other people ha also supplied them with food.—R mhael Hammond and Betsy Spruce said they had also he'ped the wife by eie- ing her fold.—Amelia Graham, defendent'a daughter, stated that for thirteen weeks her father hid only elven them 53. They hal often been ve,teoet food —Minnie Graham, defendant's wife, said her husband left her thirteen weeks ago. He had only given her 58, during that time. Only for tee kindness of the neighbours she and the children would have etarved.—Defenelant said that the week before he left hi; wife he gave her 303., and the boy gave her 7e. She came hems drunk, and took a kettle from the fire, and attempted to throw the water over him. Hs went into the scullery and she fol- lowed him with a l'r3ad knife end eruck him. She used bad language and told him to cli aa out of the Muse or she would murder him. Since he left her he had sent her 18s. He hae4 not been gone a fortnight before she Cime blackguardine hirn,and on one occasion she waited for him in the street, and threw come liehted straw which contained oil over him. Had he not been able t, take his jacket and waistcoat off, he would have been severely burned. The magistrates would see by the cap he produeed that it had been burned by the straw.—The wife denied that she did anvt+.in%, of the kind, but a neighbour who was called said she had heard that the defendant's wife did throw some lighted straw at her busband.—Defendant premised to contribute 10s.weekly towards the maintenance of hg children, and the case was adjourrel for a month in order that he might have an opportunity of doiag Co.

He pleaded not guilty.—Mr. P. R. Roberts. solicitor, who appeared for the complainant. said the assault on his cl'ent William Leigh, WAS a most serious and aggravated one. and what wee more they did not know why the assault was committed. The assault, which took place on August Bank Holiday occurred outside the "Coach and Horses" Hotel. Liverpool-road. and there were a lot of people about. his client, Leigh, was in the ' snug ' of the house and the defendant in another part. His client hqd occasion to go outside when defendant followed him and without any Provocation, his client was set noon, struck by a man, and Henson assisted in the as.ault. He was knocked on the ground kicked in the side, and was totally blind for a day and a half, and was unable to go to his work form week. —William Leigh, fiatnian, bore out his solicitor's statement. He could not suggest any reason for the assault—Thomas Lewis, labourer, Barnett street, said he was in the bar of the house at the time, and seeing some people rushing to the front. went there. He saw the complainant Leigh lying on the ground. The defendant had his foot raised as though to kick him. Witness assisted with others to take the com- plainant away.—Nancy Roscoe, 12. Dftle-strett, corroborated. Leigh. she said was in an awful state witen rescued.—The bench considered the case proved and fined Henson 10s and costs or in default 14 days.

Amen; them are certain symptoms—seen in this Cale—WiliCh so closely resemble those of censump• then as to mislead even medical men who are accus- ' tom( dto deal with lung and throat diseases. That was what happened in this instance, and it lead to wrong treatment (and neglect of the right treatment) that came near costing the life of the young girl. Owing to improved sanitation, and other reasons not to he detailed hero, there is vastly less consumption in England than there used to be ; but dyspepsia is still too common for our happiness and safety. Therefore, in all cease or illness in cid or yourig,when there is a doubt the wiser course is to take dyspepsia fer granted, and treat fur that—at least until indubitable proofs of con- sumatien show themselves. Mr. A. J. JOLLEY said the figures had been prepared at the request of the Board, and it aecmed to him that some consideratien ought to be given to them. Be did not wish to offer any adverse Cr ticism on colleagues who sat on aay of the relief committees, but he thought whatever was said ought to be said after due &libera- tion and careful thought. It was a very sr rious matter that the Board's expenditure tea out-relief had risen 35 per cent, and it bad now reached nearly £5,000 a year , for no spoarent reason. Trade was better, and the pre- sent social conditions odebt rather to point to a reduc- tion than to an increase of out-relief. It W3B a very striking fact that these figures showed that the increase ' had chiefly been in the 'mend and third districts. Thera might be a satisfactery explanation for it, but whether there was or not, he thought the figures which were now before them ought to make every member connected with those districts consider very seriously the considerations employed in administering relief. It was not a subject to be made a matter of re- crimination between members. They all bad an interest in seeing that the limey sontributed for this purpose was spent in the most carefel way. Be thought Mr. Riddette and some of his colleagues on the Newton Re. lief Committe3 might see their way to reduce the out. relief and take care that it did not rise higher. When they saw that practically the 35 per cent increase wAs in two districts with the smallest population it ought to make the Guardians think rather seriously whether there 'wag not a screw loose somewhere. The Rev. J. H. RIEDETTE said on the Nawten Relief Committee, except in the two summer months, there , was always a large committee, and every C3BB was 'thoroughly and impartially inyestigated,and they could only bring to the discharge of their duties the discreti m they possessed. Be thought it would be better if Mr. A. J. Jolley and other critical outsiders, instead ot:sr! giving instructions and unnecessary labour to h 'male an preps.' ang statistics would come over to tie com- mittee meetings,and see the distribution of out-relief for themselves. He did not mean that they should merely corn over when there was a dinner—Oeughter)—but when there was ncne,ated help the committee to investi- gate the cases, and not be continually springing these surprises upon the Beard,and holding the Newton com- mittee up to the people ot Warrington a 3 an extrava- gant body of men. Dr. Parreasow said since the new Employers Liability Bill had been passed, the colliery proprietors were dis- charging nem over a certain age. Numer.ms cases had been thrown upon the Newton Relief Committee in eon sequence, Some of the mos had not been out of work a fortnight before they appeared at the comm ttee meeting for relief.

The -1-lE;v. J. H. RIDDSTTE said hundreds of people ware being discharged at the col.eriea owing to their age,and the out-relief of the Newton Committee tended to rise still higher. The Crinut said in the Nawtoa relief district the Guar- dians were certainly at a disadvantage in net having voluntary instit itions for tne benefit of the poor. Tnere was no question that the Infirmary at Warrington saved the Holm trona assisting a considerable number. It looked very hard that in a district where many thou- sands a y( ar were paid for underground properties that no steps were taken for vilunlaray assisiag tha penile who were the means of earning that money. Mr. William Boum:mot said a number ea odtrelief cases had arisen in the Union ow:ng to ir:endly societies being unable to asiis toe aged people who had in tie r younger days paid their subscriptions and now looked for help. _ _

Mr. A. J. JOLLEY s 'id he reason su rested by the , Clerk for the out-reliof in Newton district being higher ' than in other districts was an inadequht 3 one as bearing on the point he had raised. The con along in that respect were no different to-day than they were five years ago, and it was ie that period that the increase bad taken place. It might b 3 that the predecessors of the present menthe:B were too seeere—(the Rey. J. H. Riddette : Hear, hear)—but this talk about there being no hospitals in Newt en district had no b.sring on the point. The Rev. J. H. RIDDETTE : Toe population is increae. ing, you make no allowance for that. Mr. A. J. JOLLEY : It has not increased 35 per cent, in five years. Tb 3 Rev. J. H. RIDDETTE : You must go back 10 years. Continu ng, Mr. Riddette said they had no great brewers and manufacturers in Newton diatrice ; there were only a few millionaires like Dr. Patterson who pre- sided over the relief proceedings. (Laughter:, They were wretchedly poor in their district. Mr. A. J, JOLLEY said the question of out-re if had boort raised indirectly by the classification scheme. It had been stated that the members ot the Relief Com- mittee in the Northern district could not apply the house test to people who made application for relief for the reason that they did not get decent treatment at the Workhouse. He wished to point out that wnea the Board had approved of the classification scheme that objection could not be raised any longer, and them was not the least reason for refusing to apply the house test rigiery in future. Although the expeneiture of the houel might rice, they mieht reponably expect that the expenditure on out-relief would fall. Strict admin- istration and not sentirnen'al adminittration was the best to adopt in the int rests ef the poor people them- selves. I •Mr HICKMAN stated that when he first came on that I • Bonet the :eeling throughout the ceuntry and also the utterances on that Beard were to the effect that more out-relief ought to be given. He thought that perhaps it had had something to do with the increase in the amount of cut-relief distribetee. He thought the publ c outside needed educating with respect to the adminis- tration of relief. A great many people had an idea that whatever was the cause of tee r poverty they had only to ask to receive. As the members bad sat on the relief committee they hr ow that many persons applying for out-relict hid been refused. Whilst he was in a small town in Wales he was rather surprised to see posters stating the following : " No person will be allowed out- door relief whese poverty has been caused by intemper- ate habits."

Mr. CLARKE said there was no doubt in fixes past a little more harlship W3S shown in the administraflon of out-relief. It was very probable that the mere recen- tly elect d guardians had tem a little more liberal in this respect. That was so in the district he represented.
