div.head: SUICIDE.
div.p: SUICIDE.

At the Police Station, Warrington, on Wednesday evening, Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquiry concerning the death of Winifred Jane Pemberton, aged 56 years, and who roided at 10, Stamford-street. She was found by a neighbour lying on the floor of her bedroom in a large pool of blood, with a knife beside her. Mr. Few was fore- man of the jury. Thomas Pemberton said the deceased was hls wife, living with him at 10, St imtord-street, Warrington. She was 58 years of ago. It was on Sunday night, about 10-30 that lie saw her last heforo the injaries were in- flicted. Witness was informed of the occurrence abut 3-30 on Monday afternoon whilst at work. She was gasping her last breath when he Rot horne. He knew of no reason why she should commit suicide. It was not fact that she was a won 'an of intemperate habits. He never had any suspicion of her taking her life. She suffered from varicose veins iu her legs. Minnie Pemb3rton, 17 years of age, daughter of the , deceased,2ave evidence as to going in the house on Mon- day aft ectioon,and finding her mother on the sofa. Her mottle: was not drunk bt ha I had two gills of b 2er. Witms. went to her sister's home, and when £OO re- turned home her mother was dead. She notimd noth- , jog. unusual with tor mother in toe afternoon, but she had heard Ler say that she would .do away with herseff lon several ozcasions.—Crxs exam ned by Insre3tor spinks : She did not tell her father of her Mother's threats ts take her own life. She did not think he:. mother intetd,yel to carry them out as she had threatened to do so often.

Annie Phince-tt,ii;ini..at 42, Stamfcrlstreet, stated that on Monday afternoon she was told to tell the de- ceased of an acc'dent which had occurred to hr son- In-law. She w6lked into the Et.chen, and not finding anyone, she went upstairs and found the d(c:hised be- tween two heis on the floor in one of the bedrcoma. She was lying on her back, bleeding. Witn-iss came running out screaming, and other neighbours went into the hcuse.

' Thomas Richer Ison,siated that on Monday afternoon he ca as sitting on his doorstep in company with his wife in Stamford-s'raet when he saw th 3 last witness come out of the deceased's house screaming. His wife went upstairs and he followed her. He saw the dezeased lying between two beds on her back, in a pool of blood. He immediately picked her up, and tried ta find out where she was bleeding. He saw a lot of blood about her legs and sent for a doctor. Dr. Adams arrived and witness then left. The doctor aft rwards told him that he fcund the table-knife produced in her petticoats. Mrs. Richardson gave corroborative evidence. Inspector Tail r stated that he visited the house aft,r the occurrence and saw the wound in the deceased's leg. It was an incised wound, about three iric'ies long just above the knee. There was no doubt she had been Riffer- ing severely [rem varicose veins. She had cut fght through the veins. He never saw a worse case. The knife produced was found by Dr. Adams. The jury returned a verdict that the deceaaed com- mitted suicide whilst of unsound mind.

interesting commentary upon the proceed- ings of our Council meeting of Tuesday last wh-n we discussed an imp rtant proposal by the Gas Department is to be found in the " Liverpool Echo "of Wednesday evening. In that paper is a report of the prlceedings of the Council of the neighbouring borough of South- port at which meeting the Chairman of the Southport Gas Committee anlounced amidst many apo'ogies that the Committee was only able to hand over £6,716, in aid of the rats. The Committee was severely criticized by various members presemably because the amount was so small. Would that we were in the same un-happy condition !—Yours faithfully, J. SHAW GREEN.

DR. BARNARDO'S HOMES. Sir,—Will you be so good as to allow me a brief space in your columns for the purpose of informing your numerous readers that the Christian Endeavour Societies of Warrington, Latchford, and Stockton flea.b, have arranged to take up a btreet collection on behalf of Dr. Barnardo's Homes for Waifs and Strays, on Saturday next, August 20-h. Last year, on August 21st, a similar effort was made, and the response on the part of the general public was most gratifying, a sum of £4O 12a lid being contributed. The local expenses being very small nearly the whole of this amount was sent to the homes, and duly acknowledged. When in Canada, I found upon inquiry, that almost the whole of the boys and girls emigrated to that country turn out well. The number of children in the homes is about five thousand, for whose maintenance and training an annual income of from £140,000 to £150,000 is needed. The people of Warrington will not, lam sure, be backward in doing their snare towards the financial support of these Christ Ets institutions. Duly authorised collectors, wearing official badges will be stationed at various places in the town and neigh- bourhood, and it is particularly requested that all con- tributions shall be placed in the boxes carried by such collectors. Thanking yo a frr your c iurtesy, I remain, dear Sir, faithfully yours.— (Chairman of Local Committee).

div.head: EDWARD T. REED.
div.p: EDWARD T. REED.
BAPTISMAL REGENERATION.

Sir,—! can quite understand " I ina'a " re'uttance "for the discussioa of a d gins for which he has on sympathy ;" for,it is impossinle for the questions of in- fant baptism to be discussed directly between a Catholic and a Baptist : they hays no common ground. The Baptist urges that the scripture everywhere treats faith as a pre-requisite to Baptism (at. Mark xvi. 18 : Acts 37, xvi. 30-33, &c.); the Catholic replies that these passages refer to adults only,and defends his practice as to infants by the authority of tie Church, which the I Baptist refuses to recognise. The Catholic points out that God will have all poen to be saved (I.Timathy ii. 4), aad that Baptism, the necessary condition of salvation (St. John iii, 51,m ust therefore hi attainable by all men; the Baptist repiie+ tsat Salvation is for the predestined, lad for them a'one. Thus the controversy -sanders, from one subj cc to arosher. Protestants genes- I ally rr pudiate Catholic do . trine on the plea that there esiete an obligation binding each individual to draw the subjsct matter of his faith directly from the Scriptures. It is certain that God has delivered the Scriptures to the Church with the intention that they should be read and be used as one of the sources of faith. But to whom? To each individual, that each one might fame his belief from them. This is what Protestants contend, and what Catholics justly deny. The oblig.tion of readingl the Bible, if such existed, would be rounded either in the nature of the subjeci itself or upon a positive divine , command. The nature of the subject requires only a knowledge of religion suited to each one's condition. This may be obtained in various ways, but chiefly by I the oral teaching of the Church. Nor can we point to ' any divine precept enjoining the reading of the Bible on all. Whenever the apostles addressed letters to the faithful these were intended, in the first place, for those to whom they were addressed, and were doubtless publicly read, with the necessary comments, by the pastors of those communities. Some of the inspired letters were addressed to individuals, others to par- ticular Churches. Nowhere do we find a precept enjoin- ing on all Christians, either of the times of the apostles or af later ages, the reading of the Apostolic writings. Tnis can be easily established by referring to the follow- ing authorities ; 'Vrtullian de prsescript C. 14 ; St. Augustine de doct, Christ. 1 c. 39 ; and St Jerome ep. ad. Paulin. Neither scripture nor tradition is the sole rule of faith, Inasmuch as our faith must conform with the contents of scrivisre and tradition, these two sources of faith may be callsd rules of fa:th ; but a rule of faith in the strict sense, ii that by which our under- standing of scriptures and tradition is determined. Not the scriptures alone can be this ruling principle. The same applies also to tradition taken apart from the liv- ing teaching office of the church. The truth of the exist- ence of a living teaching authority in the church,can be proved from the very attributes of scripture. This will be profitable in our rresent enquiry, especially as Pro- testants try to set up the scriptures as the only rule of faith in place of living teaching authority of the church. In order to be the sole rule of faith, the scriptures should of itself he fit to secure in the church the perpetual and unchangeable unity of the true faith, to solve with certainty the most important questions regarding our Salvation (e.g.), the necessity of baptism to ensure Salvation, the necessity WI lawfulness of infant biptism, &c. But under what conditions can the understanding of the scriptures, and with it the truths of faith, remain un- changed, the unity of faith be maintained,and the more important questions pertaining to salvation be solved from the scriptures ? Only in the case that the meaning of the scripture, at least in its most important points, is so obvious that it may be understood by all in the same way. For,as we learn from daily experienee,the opinions of men in all that does not compel assent by its evidence soon diverge. It is hardly ne7ess try to prove that scrip- ture does not pcssess such evidence ; it is, on the con- trary, very ob cure, even in mcst important points of doctrine. In fact, non-datholics in every age have sought.to prove their conflicting opinions from scripture. Hence it is impossible that scripture alone should secure the perpetuity of the christian religion, maintain unity of faith, and solve all the important problems of salva- Bien. Therefore it is impossible that it should be the sole rule of faith. But the condition of Protestantism in and out of the" church as by law established," fur- nishes the most evident proof of the insufficiency of scripture alone as a rule of faith. Since Protestantism tet up the scriptures as the sole criterion in matters of faith we perceive an ever-growing disunion; the truths of faith have been abandoned one by nne,while no means were left to check the evil—proof sufficient that unless we recognize some other rule of faith than scripture alone, neither the preservation of the deposit of faith nor the unity of the faith itself nor the security of salvation is possible. Yours &c., " SURSIIM GORDA."

P.S. I notice your correspondent with the peculiarly unfortunate pseudonym of "Quondam Schismaticus," objects to what he politely calls my "technical termino- logy," but when I real in his letter which appears in your issue of the 6th inst, that he is only taking a reckless plunge into the limitkss sea of theological con- troversy, ' lam somewhat cmsoled. I quite agree with Q. S. in his opinion "that the Catholic Faith is not always fortunate in its exponents." The Catholic faith must indeed be in a very parlous condition when it needs the defence of a member of the "Catholic Church" (Anglican) in Communion with Mr. John Kensit.

Sir,—! regret that your able correspondent" lona " has denied himself the oppirtunity of combating the detestable doctrine of Baptismal Regeneration. In order, however, that judgmmt may not go by default, I will endeavour, in my humble way, to refute the arguments of " Sursum Corda " and " Quondam Schismat,cus." But before doing so, I would remark upon the intolerant spirit displayed by " Sursum Corda." I notice. that whenever any reference is made to Roman CathOlunT, it is sure to be received by " Sursuin Corda " with " great offence," whiht he thinks lightly of the" great offence " he is giving to Protestants when parading his rank Romanism. However, the less said about "offence" the better, for advocates who cannot give and take are of no use ; and I can assure " Sursurn Corda " .that I shall not spare him. The remark of your ecclesias- tical correspondent about the Baptists will apply with equal force to all Protestants, viz, that there is no com- mon ground between them. Roman Catholicism is simply a, system of idolatry, and Chr:stianity is a spirit- ual religion. Thu4between the material and the spiritual there can be nothing in common. Further,there can be no common ground in this respect—that I take my stand an idle Bible, whilst "Sursum Corda " takes his upon "the church and tradition." Again he is all for authority, and,, So I I am for" the libgrty wherewith Christ makes U free. Tight go on. The Bible is a for- s bidden book to Romanists, and consequently priests and people gen-rally know nothing of it. Only casuists like " who belong to the Romanist Press Bureau," S u r sd h Cv oe r ada knowledge of it.and that only such as n suits their purpose. This 13 evidenced by the fact that 4igursum Cord& " can only quote one passage of Scrip- ture in support of his doctrine : that baptism is essential to salvation. Now I assert that the essential t 3 salva- tion is not baptism but belief in the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. Throughout the New restanient there are numerous passages to support my contention, and I will only quote a few of them. (1) " Be it known unto you, therefor?, men and brethren, that through this man is Preached unto you the forgiveness of sins, and by him all that believe are justified from all things." (2) " • - . and said. Sirs, what must I do to be saveg? And they said,helieve on the Lord Josus Christ,and thou shall be saved." (3) te If thou shalt confeSS!alith thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God loath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved." There are here no references to baptism 0 all, and therefore baptism is not an essential to salvation, ner.in- deed can be,for a spiritual religion requires neither rites

ear ceremonies. Having thus disposed of ths essential- ity of baptism,l new address myself to the abiurd doc- trine of baptismal regeneration, and assert that baptists has no regenerative efficacy. In support of this asser- tion,l will quote the phrase of"Quoadam S;hisceaticus:" " Repent and be baptised." Here, my riders will ob- serve that the preliminary is " repentance," and it is this act,and not baptism, that involveq he regen.rative agency. Again there is the passage "He that believeth and is baptised shall be saved ; but he that believeth Act shall be damned." You will notice that this pas- sage does not state that the unbapti4ed are damned but the unbelievers;therefore the baptism is unnecessary and unavailing. Whet the scriptures plainly teach is that the regenerative agency is what Protestants commonly describe as conversion. Your con erpondent "Quondam Schismaticus "seems to kick at this term and says that it simply means being brought into ieiation with God. I assert that it means more and that is a complete inward change. " That ye put off concerning the former conversation the old man which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts ; and be renewed in the spirit of your mind ; and that ye put on the new man which after God is created in righteousness and true hoiiness." All this is effecte I, not by baptism but by repentance and faith, and thus baptismal regeneration has no foundation in the Bible.

Admitting however, for the sake of argument, the validity of baptism,then I maintain,as against"Quodam Schismaticus" that infants or children are not the proper subjects of it. I have already quoted passages to show that with baptism there is attached the prior condition of repentance and belief, and as infants are incapable of fulfilling these conditions, it is obvious they are not qualified for its observation. In illustration of my con- tention I could cite the whole of the New Testament cases, but I will contcnt myself with the case of the Apostle Paul. As to" Sursum Corda's " argument respecting the " living teaching authority of the Churzh,' we Protes- tants regard this as so muca humbug. Throughout the scriptures there is no rPference to any such powerful in-taution as he refers t 3 wrien he mentioas " the church." In apostolic times there was not one church but several, these being the gatherings of small com- panies of believers wh3 set up their churches anywhere as they pie ism], and who were not under the authority or d msination of any other comraly or bode. In reading and expounding th I scriptures, we Protestants are oleo following apnst dic usage, and, "Sursum Corda" notwithstanding, we give every person liberty to in- terpret the scriptures according to his ability. In doing so iv, fail to " perceive an over.rrowing disunion." On the contrary we recognise that, while allowing every sect its fre thin of interpretation, on fundamental principle we are all at oae, and in nothing more so than in r.osisting the encroachments of a soul-blighting, liberty-destroying Romanism as expounded By "Sursum Corda."—Yours, Sze,

THE COUNCIL AND URBLN POWERS. With regard to the application of the Council for Urban Powers, the Clerk read a communication from the Local Government Board stating that they deemed it necessary for an enquiry to be held by 03i5 of their Inspectors, and asked the Council to state where the enquiry could be most conveniently held. The Clerk added that if the enquiry were hell the Council would have to show that there was sufficient reason for con- verting the district into an urban district,by evidence of the existence of places which should come under their control.

The CHAIRMAN said he thought they would not be able to prove their miss. The Council decided to postpone the application for the present, and the Clerk was mitructed to write to the Local Government Board to that effect.

div.head: A. WA.ItRINGTON 114. N DItOWNED IN
div.p: A. WA.ItRINGTON 114. N DItOWNED IN
THE SHIP CANAL.

On Mon.,a,y morning about half-past eight a body was picked out of the Matiche,,ter Ship Canal about 200 yards from the Acton Grange lay-by. The body was re- moved to Moore Smithy, and an inquiry was conducted by Mr. Woreley at the Red Lion Inn, Moore,on Tuesday afternoon respecting the deceased. The first witness called was Thornal O'Brien, 5, Platt. street, Warrington, a tanner,who identified the deceased as his brother, and whose name was John O'Brien. He was 28 years of age and was a general labourer. Wit- ness last saw his brother alive on Monday night,August Bth. He then told witness that he intended to walk to Chester the following day, and was desirous of getting up early in order to do so. His object in getting to Chester was to draw some money which was owing him. Deceased was an unmarried man, and had no troubls on his mind to cause him to commit suicide. Witness could only account for his brother being found near Acton Grange from the fact that he worked there during the construction of the Ship Canal, and might have gone there with the object of finding work. Henry Cole, a bridgeman in the employ of the Ship Canal Company at Moore deposed that be saw the body floating in the water. With the agsistan:e of a man named Pearce be got the body to the banks of the canal, and gave information to the police. P.C. Ellis stationed at Moore stated that he removed the body to the place where it now lay. Thera was a mark on the face which was of a superficial character, and in his opinion it was caused after death. The body appeared to have been in the water about a week, and he believed it had been disturbed by a passing steamer. Nothing was found in the pockets of the deceased. Captain Waring said a great many people went down to the lay-by at Acton Grange to get work, and the de- ceased might have done the same, and fallen into the canal.
The Coroner said that seemed to be the only supposi- tion.
The jury returned a verdict that th 3 deceased was found drewned.

Sil- cock, however, maintailed his Mm defenc,, and though all efforts were made to tempt him to hit none were succr Hampson quickly hit three boundaries and a single and was then caught in two minds with the u3ual result. Seven o'clock arrived without further disaster, Silcozk taking out his bat for nine.

Turning to the doings of the second eleven who 03C11- pied the Areley ground, and had the second team from Cheadle Elulmo as their opponents, the Warringtoniani who were the first to go to the wickets compiled the very respectable score of 189. An excellent E tot was made, the initial batsmen—Adamson and Crsmpton— staying together until 80 runs had been recorded on ne telegraph beard. Adamson was the first player to make his return to the pavilion, and was rather unforzunate in being stumped just as he was nearing his balf-centrry, he having contributed 47 of the 80 runs sire sdy men- tioned. This proved to be the top seers of tin afternoon. On the Warrington side Crompton was the next highest surer with 26 to his credit. It ibexes had the misfortune to twist his knee when he had sco:ed 17, and was obliged to retire owing to his injuries, The Warrington score was augmented by 19 extras, which shows ih It there were some weak points in the attack of the visitors. The first four batsmen of the Cheadle Hulme tsam all reached doutsle figures, the most successful bowler on the Warrington side being Howard who took three wickets for 18 runs. When stumps were drswn the visitore had compiled 113 runs for the loss of only five wickets.

The Sankey Wira Mills first team again asserted its superiority as a local amateur eleven by defeating Grap- penhall St. Wilfrid's at Grappenhall. Going in first the win men placed 54 runs to their credit, 15 of which came from the bat of H. Cook. Grappeahall when called upon to exceed this comparatively small score failed to do so,and the team was dismissed for 34 runs. It was the bowling on each side that was a feature of the match. For the winners, Simpson added to his reputa- tion as a bowler by taking five wickets for eleven runs. On the other side Warburton ran him closely for honours by securing five wickets for 16 runs. Bath are highly creditable performances. I understend that the Sankey Wire Mills team has yet to receive its first de- feat this season at the hands at a local eleven. The only defeat inflicted on them WAS that sustained against Bir- kenhead Grosvenor who pay a visit to Warrington on Saturday. From all I hear there is a determination on the part of the wire men to avenge that defeat to-day.

div.head: CYCLING.
div.p: CYCLING.

A cycling incident —tia;--ci-itails of which border on the marvellous, has occurred at Tuxford, Newark. A young lady was cyc ing down a steep hill when, owing to her feet slipping off the pedals, she lost control of the machine, and ran at a furious rate in the direction of a cottage standing at the foot of the hill,the door of which was closed. A serious accident appeared imminent when events took an unexpected turn. At the critical moment the door was opened by the occupier—an old lady—and the bicycle and rider, pursuing their headlong course, entered the domicile and collided with the old lady, knocked her backwards into the room. tier daughter, who rushed forward, met with a similar fate, and toe runaway bicycle, after overturning furniture and crockery,deposited its fair rider on the floor of the apart- ment. !Sloppily none of the panies were much the worse for tteir exciting experience.

-- At South Shield; on Monday, an inquest was held on John Hilton, paintar, who died from injuries received while cycling. Evidence was given that Hilton and a companion were proeteiing at four miles an h3ur, and were on their right side of the road, when Arci-wr John Wilson, coming in the opposite direction,endeavouredto pass with his machine batween them, but collided with Hilton. Wilson said he had been cyciing ten years, and did no; know the left was the proper side of the road. The jury found the injuries were caused by the careless rtding of Wilson.

-- Mr. R.L.Jefferson,v;h3 is ridiag to IChiva on a bicycle. has safely reached Orenburg, at the extreme point of East Russia. Since leaving Eagland he has covered 4,181 miles in a little over three months. He h3pe3 to reach Rhin before the end of the month.

.A. A. Chas, the celebrated North-road cyclist, acc nn- phshed one of the grandest performances of his career at the Cryitalralace on Wedneaday. With a flying s.art he covered tin miles in 17mins. 20sec.—a time which constitutes a reicond for the conditions under which it vras made, and which demonstrates that he is quite capable of lowering J. W. Stocks' standing-start record of 17mins. 47 1-53ec. Eight seconds is a liberal allow- ance for the value of a flier" ; and this makes .out Chase to be about 19sec. better than Stacks at ten Mlles.

SINGULAR STORY BY A WARRINGTON MAN. At Crewe on Tuesday atternoon. Richard Hoare,a young man, of Warrington, was charged with wan- dering abroad and not being able to give a good account of himself. Police-constable Cogger said that the prisoner was brought to the police station that morning by Mr. Jones, of Willaston. He had a cut on his throat, which was covered with con- gealed blood. He said he had been with some elec- tricians during the night, and that they had been trying to kill him by electricity. He had escaped from them, and then a number of Volunteers had threatened to shoot him. To prevent that he had tried Co kill himself. Ile handed to the police a knife, with which he said he had cut his throat.— He was remanded in custody.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EA.RLESTOWN.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EA.RLESTOWN.
[BY A COURRSPONDENT

The vexed question of school ac-commodation stills keeps to the front at Earlestown, Mr. Sarni Woods broached the subject in the House of Com- mons last week, but I am afraid be has been sup- plied with information which is not exactly correct, or is sotnewhat exaggerated. What Mr. Woods meant by siying that free schooling could not be obtained unless the children walke I nearly a mile further,l do not know. Free schooling is obtain- able in Esrlestown at the District School, and also at Wargrave,and perhaps it is Wargrave school Mr. Woods alludes to. Mr. Hanbury doss not know everything about the matter eitner, when he says there will be plenty of free school accommodation when the new school is built. There may be at one end of the town, but the other portions remain as at present. The great stumbling block is the Wes- leyan school,which still charges fees,and until some arrangement is made by woich the fees can be abolished, this wilt always be a source of com- plaint.

I sea Dr. Valentine on behalf of the Ambulance Committee has offered to hand over to the District Council the ambulance litter which is housed near the Co-operative Society's premise 4, and to which I drew attention sone short time ago, stating that its condition was a di,grace. Dr. Valentine has taken the wisest course po-sib!e under the circum- stances, and when once it has been put into proper usable condition, the Council will doubtless see that it is kept in a fit wets for usa. I should have pre- ferred that the Committee would sell the litter and devote the money realised towards the purchase of a new one constructed on the most modern principle. The present one is undeniably old-fashioned,and in addition is a most uncomfortable vehicle to ride upon.

At last the Council have recognised that there is a dearth of magistrates in the Newton Petty Sessional division. This is a fact which has been pateat to anyone frequenting the Police Court for a considerable time, and the business of the Court has had to suff.r in csusequence. Steps are to be taken to bring the qtvstion under the notice ot the Chairman of the Bench, and perhaps through his influence some improvement may ba effected.

Dr. Watkins treated the pollution of Newton lake very Mildly in his report ,on the health of the district. lie said the late the late spring and cool summer had been of advantage to us, as otherwise the lake might have developed a dangerous nuisance. Nothing more! Only a nuisance ! I have had several oppprtunities of experiencing the disagreeable effluvia emanating from the lake and my opinion is that something more than a nuisance will be developed it an improvement is not soon effected. The Council is evidently taking proper steps to secure this end, and it is hoped their efforts will be early attended with success.

TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION IN CHESUIRE. Mr. It. P. Ward, the organising secretary of the work of the Tecbnical Instruction Committee of the Cheshire County Council, has reported to the C"11- oil the work done by that committee during the ' past year. The report shows that in Cae,hire there , are thirty-seven Town Council:a and Urban District Councils. Nineteen of these either levy a rate or , make a grant out of the rates in aid of technical in- struction in their respective districts, the amount so raised being £3,532 7s. Bd. Daring the year these nineteen authorities have received grants amount- ing to £4,002 Ios., an increase of £5OO over the pre- ceding year. Altogether there was £8,933 25. 8,1 available for technical instruction purposes in the urban districts of the county. The organising secre- tary sets forth in detail the work of the year. There are many proofs, he points out, that the efforts put forth to improve dairy products, and to bring more enlightened and scientific methods and ideas to bear upon agricultural work generally, are gradu- ally bearing good fruit. Thera could,however,be no real stoppage to the educational waste in our present system until the age for exemption from attendance at the elementary school was materially raised,aad provision made for attendcnce thereafter regularly for some years at evening continuation Schools. The third and last day's shooting in connection with the 38th annual meeting of the above associa- tion took place on Saturday at Altcar. There wai a large crowd of visitors, and the weather was again favourable. The Lird Liewenant's competi- tion, which was that for in two ttiges, was the principal event on the programtue. In the firet instance the 269 competitors who took part in the contest, as against 273 at the previous meetiag,fired seven shots at 200, 500, and 600 yards, anti those who made the fifty best scores in the first stage won their places to shoot in the second round. At 500 and 600 yards in the second stage, where the con- testants fired ten shots at each distance, some big Iscoring was witnessed. At the shorter range, Private Thomasson (Ist Liverpool) Private Wat- mough (Ist Liverpool), of Beamont-street,Warring- ton, and Private Munroe (3rd Liverpool) scored the highest possible number of points. At the next range the shooting was very close. Armoury- Sergeant Wright (2nd Lincashire Fusiliers) and Private Watmough(lst Liverpool) finished with the best aggregates of 192 to their credit. At this time Thomasson had brought up his score to 190, and, with a shot to go, he only wanted a magpie to win. The excitement then became very intense. After a brief interval Thomasson fired again, and, scoring the magpie, he beat his opponents by one point. Private Watmough, who was formerly a member of the Warrington corps, resides in Beamont-street, and is one of the best known shots in the country. He first joined th 3 volunteers in 1867 as a drummer lad, and has been indentified with almost every in- strument in the band. For many years he figured prominently at the National rifle meetings at Wimbledon and Bislev.and has occasionally figured in the Queens 300. His chief successes have how- ever been scored at Altcar, and his latest success which brings with it a prize of £lo,will be welcome news to Warrington volunteers.
RAILWAY COLLISION AT THE CAPE . TWENTY NATIVES ROASTED TO DEATH. • CAPEYOWN, WEDNESDAY.

A terrible railway accident, resulting in ne loss of fiitsen lives and injury to a number of people, occurred last night near Matjesfontein, in Worcester County Cape Colony. The train involved was the mail train from Johannesburg. It was standing on the line when a runa- way goods train—which by some strange oversight had been allowed to get on to the same line of rails—dashed into it with fcarful force. The first part of train was completely wrecked by th 3 collibiort, and the piled-up wreckage caught fire from the scattered embers of the locomotive's furnace.

The first r3ports unhappily under-estimated the extent of the disaster and its appalling accompaniments. No fewer than twenty Kaffirs were burned to death amongst the blazing wreckage, and five others were more merci- fully killed by being crushed in the ruins before the fire reached them.

The injured passengers have been brought into Cape Town by special train and ara now under medical treat- ment in the hospital. Most of them are doing well, and it is hoped that all will recover, although some of the cases are serious.

nos survivots state that the scene as the wreckage of the great train blazed in the darkness of the night on the solitary desert was one absolutely frightful in its horror. All that was left of the wrecked passenger cars was a great pile of ashes and the charred remains of human bodies.

Hints on Cooking Corn Flour. Notwithstanding the wide use of Corn Flour, particularly in summer, as a cool and refreshing Blanc-mange, many fail to bring out its true and delicate flavour. To thoroughly enjoy a Blanc-mange : FIRST.—Make wholly with good sweet milk without any addition of water, and do not use too much Corn Flour. (24 ozs of BROWN & TOLSON'S "PATENT" Corn Flour to two pints milk is the right proportion.) SECOND.—BIend the Corn Flour with a little of the milk, bring the rest to the boil, take off the fire, and add the Corn Flour slowly. THIRD.—Then boil well, in fact, boil down to three-fourths of the original bulk, which will take about ten minutes' boiling. To use warm, turn out when cold, and reheat in the oven. FOURTH,—And above all, use only and always the recognised best— BROWN & POLSON'S "PATENT" CORN FLOUR. It is more delicate in flavour and goes further than others. One pound of Brown & Poison's Corn Flour will make twelve one-pint puddings. Thus the cost of the Corn Flour in a pudding is so small, that everyone can afford to have the best. Ask for BROWN & POLSON'S CORN FLOUR —"PATENT" is their BEST QUALITY—and be sure that you get it.
